item.title: Affordability Is a Freight Problem
item.content:encoded:
"Affordability" is the word of the season. A Wall Street Journal survey, unpacked in a three-part October essay series by a free-market economist, found large majorities in both parties backing caps, controls and subsidies. For carriers, brokers, 3PLs and freight forwarders this isn't an abstract debate: the price level sets what diesel and equipment cost, what your customers can afford, and how long they take to pay you.

🛣️ Many High Costs Are Written into the Rules

  • The survey numbers are striking capping credit card interest at 10% won 78% of Democrats, 83% of Republicans and 76% of independents, and limiting rent increases to 5% above inflation drew 65% support overall. The essay's point is that price, wage and rent controls have led to rationing, lines, black markets and corruption every time they've been tried.
  • The core argument: government can't make things "more affordable" overall by taxing, spending, borrowing or regulating. It can only shift who pays. Subsidies against fixed supply, like energy and housing, just push prices higher.
  • The proposed fixes land right on freight: drop ethanol requirements (which the essay says add about 30 cents a gallon to diesel), abolish the Jones Act (blamed for higher transport costs), eliminate tariffs, allow automated ports, reform environmental permitting, and keep deregulating.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: A cost built into a rule tends to stick, because the few who benefit are organized and the many who pay are scattered. In our world, the many are small fleets, their shippers, and the SMEs downstream. A policy-made cost can also change with one vote, so price lanes and write contracts with that uncertainty in mind.

📈 Higher Prices Don't Come Back Down

  • The consumer price index is 27% higher than just before inflation hit in January 2021, and 14% higher than it would be if inflation had stayed at 2% the whole time.
  • The Fed treats its "price stability" mandate as 2% inflation forever and lets bygones be bygones. Even "transitory" inflation means permanently higher prices.
  • Inflation creates churn: some gain, some lose. People on fixed nominal incomes fall behind, and anyone who held government bonds lost about 14% to inflation.
  • The proposed alternative is a real price-level or long-run-average target. That would also commit Congress to repaying its debt without inflation, which takes away a fiscal source of inflation pressure.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Think of a freight invoice as a small bond you've issued to your customer: a fixed number of dollars, paid later. When it isn't clear that government borrowing will be backed by future budgets, the price level adjusts upward, and anyone holding fixed-dollar claims absorbs the loss. That includes bondholders, long-term contracts and your receivables. The longer your terms, the more of that risk you carry.

🏛️ Why Price "Fixes" Stay Popular

  • Bedrock principle: don't transfer income by distorting prices. Political reality: income gets transferred by distorting prices, partly because it lets politicians favor a constituency without the visibility of taxing one group and mailing checks to another.
  • In any single negotiation, price is an income transfer, so people assume forcing everyone's prices down makes everyone better off. What they miss is that handing out subsidies widely drives prices up even further.
  • The unseen gets ignored: the people who can't get an apartment at all, the apartments that never got built. And the "fallacy of composition" means what's good for one household or business isn't always good for the whole economy.
  • The essay's remedy: institutions and limits on government work as precommitments that protect good outcomes from the latest price spike.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Freight runs on negotiated prices. When relief, mandates or caps get decided politically, they tend to reach the best-connected interests first, and the cost moves to someone else's balance sheet. Often that's a customer who quietly runs short of cash. Late payments are the "unseen" in trucking: they don't show up on the P&L until they turn into a bad debt.

🔬 The Research Lens: Forecasts Hinge on Assumptions

  • A 2017 Journal of Monetary Economics paper notes that many standard models predict a deep recession with deflation when interest rates hit zero. They also make odd policy predictions: useless government spending, technical regress, capital destruction and forward guidance can all raise output.
  • The paper shows these predictions depend heavily on which equilibrium you assume. For the same interest-rate path, the alternative solutions predict mild inflation, small output swings and negative multipliers.
  • Fiscal policy considerations favor those milder outcomes. That's a reminder that expectations about government budgets, not just the central bank's rate, shape the result.

Why it matters to freight and insurance : If expert macro forecasts swing this much depending on the assumptions, a credit decision shouldn't rest on one headline outlook. Plan for a range of outcomes and protect the tail : the key customer who doesn't pay.

🧾 Getting Paid Is Now the Risk Conversation

  • Allianz Trade expects global business insolvencies to rise 5% in 2026, the fifth straight yearly increase and 24% above the pre-pandemic average. U.S. insolvencies are forecast to rise 8%.
  • One credit specialist told Insurance Business that payments that used to land 3–4 days after departure now take 1–2 weeks.
  • Underwriters cut or pull buyer limits as risk worsens. Coface warned that getting cover "after the point can be challenging." Act early.
  • Credit insurance covered €9.58 trillion of trade in 2025, and insured receivables help banks lend more, on better terms.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Trade credit insurance turns your receivables, often your largest asset, into a protected asset that can strengthen your borrowing base. And the best time to put cover in place is before your customer's name shows up on a watch list.

💡 Final Thought

The affordability debate will keep producing caps, relief programs and new rules. The higher price level is largely here to stay, and who pays for it is often settled by whoever has the most pull. You can't control either one. You can control who you extend credit to, on what terms, and whether a customer's failure becomes your failure. As a TRS and TCS with six years in transportation insurance, I help trucking, logistics and insurance SMEs see that risk early and protect the cash flow they've earned.

📞 Let's Talk

Want a second look at your customer concentration, payment terms or credit exposure? Or curious how trade credit insurance could support your working capital? Reach out for insights, risk management advice or insurance solutions.

item.title: To quote Hank Williams "You are just in time to be too late"
item.content:encoded:
The call usually starts the same way. The driver checked in on time. Then the truck sat: no door, a shift change, a full yard. Three hours later the trailer is empty, the driver's hours are nearly gone, and the next receiver is asking where the truck is. Fleet owners ask a simple question: if we arrived on time, can the trucking company or the broker still get hit financially?

The short answer is yes, not always in the way people expect.

On the stop where your driver actually made the appointment, the major retail programs I reviewed generally measure "on time" at the gate, not when the last pallet comes off the trailer. Kroger's official 2025 vendor-compliance update defines on-time delivery as the purchase order being gated in at the distribution center on the Original Requested Arrival Date. The 3 percent ORAD compliance fee applies only to late purchase orders caused by the vendor. A separate $200 fee applies when a shipment is more than 30 minutes late to the scheduled appointment at gate-in. Many of those fees also do not apply when Kroger manages the inbound lane. A slow unload after a timely gate-in should not, by itself, trigger those late-arrival charges.

Walmart's on-time measure is described the same way by trade sources that work inside supplier portals. If a delivery appointment was scheduled, the Arrival Gate Timestamp is treated as the Arrival Compliance Date. If no appointment was booked, Walmart may use the "Pro Date," the day it processes the shipping paperwork, which can be days after the truck arrived. That is a documentation problem, not an unloading problem. Those Walmart details come from consultant reporting, not a public Walmart page, and should be confirmed in Retail Link.

So why do fleets still lose money when the dock is the delay?

First, detention. The truck is still sitting, and the hours-of-service clock is still running. ATRI's September 2024 study found that 52 percent of truckload drivers ran out of available on-duty time at a customer facility because of detention at least once in 2023. Waiting is not free, even when it is not the carrier's fault.

Second, the cascade. Detention at Stop 1 makes the driver late to Stop 2. ATRI reported that 57.8 percent of truckload drivers were late to, or had to cancel, a later pickup or delivery at least once in 2023 because they were detained at the previous facility. The fine, if there is one, often attaches to the second appointment, not the facility that caused the wait.

Third, collection is weak. ATRI found that 94.5 percent of fleets charge detention fees, but carriers invoice only 75 percent of incidents, and only 55 percent of those invoices are paid. For truckload fleets, fees were collected on just 43.5 percent of all detention incidents. The median truckload fee was $50 an hour, against $99.54 in non-fuel revenue per hour. A carrier may also be unable to bill detention if the driver was late to the appointment, even if the wait that followed was much longer.

Fourth, some broker and shipper contracts deduct a late fee from the settlement whether or not the carrier caused the delay. Owner-operators have described $250 late-arrival deductions in rate confirmations. Those are examples, not an industry average, but the contract language is what matters.

In 2018, the U.S. Department of Transportation's Office of Inspector General estimated that a 15-minute increase in average dwell time raises the expected crash rate by 6.2 percent. It also associated detention with $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion in reduced driver earnings and $250.6 million to $302.9 million in reduced carrier net income in the for-hire truckload sector. I did not find a 2024 through 2026 federal law that sets detention-time standards. A truck-parking grant bill has been introduced, and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration is collecting new detention data and has proposed a limited pilot that would let participating drivers pause the 14-hour window, including for detention. Until then, this remains a contract and documentation problem.

Standard auto and motor truck cargo policies generally will not pay a late fee, a missed-appointment deduction, or a retailer's OTIF chargeback. Cargo forms commonly exclude delay, loss of use, and loss of market, and some also exclude contractual fines. Auto liability is built for injury and property damage from an accident, not a service-failure penalty in a rate confirmation. If a customer contract passes those charges through to the carrier, that exposure is usually uninsured.

What I tell the fleets I work with is practical. Keep the record that proves you were on time: the appointment confirmation, the ELD and geofence arrival timestamp, the gate-in or guard-shack time, and a note if the dock was not ready. If a receiver later scores the load late, or a broker deducts a fee, that file is the dispute. Review detention clauses before you haul the freight: when the clock starts, what "carrier-controllable" means, and whether a chargeback can be passed through regardless of cause. Do not assume a timely arrival will be obvious later, and do not assume insurance will close the gap. It usually will not.

If your drivers are arriving on time and still leaving a facility behind on hours, money, or the next appointment, it is worth a closer look at the contracts and the paper trail. I am always glad to talk it through.

#Trucking #Freight #Insurance #SupplyChain #FleetManagement

item.title: Carriers, Capacity, and the Next Level of Trucking Logistics
item.content:encoded:
An analysis incorporating industry developments, game-theoretic dynamics, and the thesis that operating carriers—not large logistics intermediaries—will drive the next wave of innovation in trucking and logistics.

Introduction

Craig Fuller, founder and CEO of FreightWaves, recently argued that the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s enforcement crackdown is effectively permanent. Small carriers and brokers hoping for a future loosening of rules should not expect relief, he said, because the industry’s largest fleets now want tighter standards. “Follow the money,” Fuller stated at Optym’s Convergence 2026 conference. The largest motor carriers, along with the American Trucking Associations and the Truckload Carriers Association, view stricter driver-hiring standards as “desperately needed” and “the only way that they will survive.”

Reporting over the past year shows a combination of deliberate industry support for tougher rules, large carriers and brokers actively shrinking the pools of carriers they will use, and technical problems with FMCSA’s new Motus registration system that have grounded thousands of mostly small operators. The result has been a measurable reduction in available capacity, even as freight demand has remained relatively soft.

This pattern is best understood not as a conspiracy but as a Nash equilibrium of aligned incentives. At the same time, a distinct thesis deserves attention: the operating carriers themselves—not the large third-party logistics (3PL) and fourth-party logistics (4PL) organizations—are the ones positioned to drive genuine innovation that takes trucking and logistics to the next level. Larger intermediary organizations are, by nature, slower to adopt, more inclined to hold back disruptive change, and better equipped to use financial strength and marketing position to crush competitors.

Motus and the Suspension Wave

Motus, FMCSA’s new registration system , went live for all carriers in mid-May 2026, replacing key functions of the older Portal and Unified Registration System. It was designed to strengthen identity verification, confirm principal places of business, and help identify “chameleon” carriers that shut down and reopen under new names to evade enforcement. FMCSA officials have said the system is keeping thousands of people out of the industry as part of broader anti-fraud efforts. At the same time, the rollout has produced widespread technical problems.

In late October 2026 , analysis by the Central Analysis Bureau and Commercial Carrier Journal found that more than 6,475 companies had their bodily-injury and property-damage insurance requirements changed—often from $750,000 or below to $1 million or higher—triggering involuntary suspensions. Roughly 6,000 of those changes occurred in a short period around October 27. One documented case involved Dynamic MD, a long-standing Illinois flatbed and step-deck carrier that was erroneously reclassified as a hazmat operator. Its authority was suspended, it lost the ability to book loads, and it received no advance notice. Similar insurance-related and administrative glitches produced large monthly spikes in suspension orders after Motus launched: approximately 1,848 in May, 5,518 in June, 3,559 in July, 4,539 in August, and 6,249 in September.

FMCSA Chief Safety Officer Steve Dowling has acknowledged that roughly 5 percent of registration activity has faced problems while emphasizing that Motus is performing its intended screening function. Separately, the agency has removed more than 10,000 commercial driver training providers from its registry since December 2025. For many small fleets, even a temporary inactive status is enough to lose freight, because brokers and shippers routinely check authority before tendering loads.

Large Carriers and Brokers Shrink Their Approved Lists

At the same time, major carriers and brokers have been deliberately reducing the number of carriers they will work with. Schneider National cut its brokerage approved-carrier network from 60,000 to 14,000—a reduction of roughly 77 percent. The process began partly in response to cargo theft and expanded under stricter safety and liability standards. CEO Jim Filter has said there are not 100,000 carriers that major players would consider safe enough to use. Schneider executives have described the capacity squeeze as ongoing and supportive of better rates into 2027.

Knight-Swift has reduced its approved brokerage carrier pool by about 70 percent over roughly two years. CEO Adam Miller has cited cargo theft, highway safety, and broker liability as reasons for tighter screening, including a requirement of at least one year of operating history. C.H. Robinson has also been trimming its carrier base following the Supreme Court’s Montgomery decision and a large jury verdict against the company in a negligent-hiring case. Owner-operators have reported being locked out of load boards and told they no longer meet the broker’s updated criteria.

These reductions are not marginal. They remove tens of thousands of carriers from the pools that actually receive freight from large shippers and brokers, regardless of whether those carriers remain active in FMCSA systems.

Regulatory Exits and Industry Support

Broader enforcement has removed substantial capacity. Reports citing carrier executives and agency data put the figures at roughly 40,000 non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses revoked or not reissued, more than 29,000 English-language proficiency out-of-service orders, and approximately 10,000 training providers closed or removed. Multiple states have ended or sharply curtailed non-domiciled CDL programs after federal audits and the final rule that took effect in March 2026. English-language proficiency enforcement has continued to accelerate, with FMCSA reporting tens of thousands of out-of-service orders since mid-2025.

The American Trucking Associations and allied groups have publicly supported these directions. In late 2025, ATA, the Truckload Carriers Association, and dozens of state trucking associations released a comprehensive action plan targeting non-domiciled CDLs, English proficiency, fraud, chameleon carriers, and ELD integrity. ATA leadership has written to legislators calling for additional reforms to ensure drivers are “properly qualified, adequately trained, and legally operating in the country.” Large-carrier executives have repeatedly described the crackdown as still in its early or middle stages and as a positive for capacity discipline, even with muted freight volumes. Elevated tender rejection rates—reported in the 11–12 percent range in some periods—despite soft demand have been cited as evidence of the supply-side effect.

Aligned Incentives and Nash Equilibrium

The record does not show a single coordinated campaign, but it does show aligned incentives. Large asset carriers and the trade associations that represent them have concluded that the surge of low-cost, non-compliant capacity that entered during and after the pandemic boom undercut their economics. They are not lobbying for a return to lower barriers. At the same time, liability pressure after Montgomery and the CH Robinson verdict gives large brokers clear reasons to shrink their approved lists. Motus adds a technical overlay: intentional blocking of suspected bad actors plus widespread glitches and reclassifications that have produced thousands of involuntary suspensions in short periods.

This is a classic Nash equilibrium outcome. Each major player is optimizing for its own interests given what the others are doing. No single large player has a strong incentive to reverse course unilaterally. If Schneider or Knight-Swift re-expands its approved list while others stay strict, it re-exposes itself to cargo theft, fraud, and liability without gaining a lasting rate advantage. The safer (and currently more profitable) move is to stay selective. Smaller carriers cannot unilaterally force their way back onto the major lists. Their best individual options are compliance, niching, or exiting—none of which reverses the broader equilibrium.

Because no major player improves its position by switching alone, the tighter screening and reduced small-carrier access persist. Independent self-interested action plus aligned goals produce emergent coordination. You do not need a coordinated plot to explain why small carriers are being squeezed from multiple directions at once.

The Carrier-Led Innovation Thesis

A personal perspective that deserves serious consideration is that the operating carriers—the companies that actually run trucks, manage drivers, and move freight—are the ones who will bring about the innovation that takes trucking and logistics to the next level. Larger organizations, particularly large 3PLs and 4PLs, are by nature slow to move and adopt. They will hold back innovation and use their financial strength and marketing position to crush anybody they want.

Carriers sit closest to the operational realities: equipment utilization, driver retention, route efficiency, maintenance costs, customer service at the dock, and the daily friction of compliance. Innovations that matter—whether in telematics integration, dynamic routing that accounts for real detention patterns, predictive maintenance that reduces roadside failures, or new models for driver pay and scheduling—tend to emerge from operators who feel those problems directly. Large intermediary organizations often layer on complexity, extract margin, and prefer solutions that protect their existing relationships and technology stacks rather than disrupt them.

History in trucking supports this pattern. Many of the practical advances in safety technology, fuel efficiency, and capacity management originated with asset-based carriers or owner-operators who had skin in the game, not with pure brokers or logistics consultants. Large 3PLs and 4PLs excel at aggregation, visibility platforms, and contract logistics, but their incentive structure favors stability and scale over rapid experimentation. When a smaller or mid-sized carrier develops a better way of doing something, the larger organizations can (and often do) use superior capital, existing customer relationships, and marketing muscle to replicate or marginalize it.

The current equilibrium of tighter screening and capacity discipline may actually create space for this carrier-led innovation. As the pool of marginal or non-compliant capacity is reduced, the remaining carriers that can operate reliably have more opportunity to differentiate on service, technology, and efficiency rather than pure price. Those who invest in real operational improvements—not just compliance theater—stand to capture share from both the large intermediaries and the carriers that fail to adapt.

This does not mean large logistics organizations will disappear. It means the next meaningful advances in how freight actually moves are more likely to come from the carriers who live with the consequences of those advances every day. Larger organizations will adopt what works once it is proven, and they will use their resources to scale or suppress what threatens their position. The innovators, however, will be the carriers.

Implications

For small and mid-sized carriers, the practical result of the current environment has been fewer opportunities to get freight, higher barriers to entry or re-entry, and operational disruptions from system errors that can take days or weeks to correct. For large asset-based carriers, the same conditions have been described as overdue capacity discipline that should support higher rates and market share as 2027 bids approach. Fuller’s “follow the money” framing is consistent with the public statements, list reductions, and regulatory outcomes reported over the past year.

The Nash equilibrium of aligned incentives explains the durability of the squeeze without requiring conspiracy. At the same time, the carrier-led innovation thesis suggests that the same environment may reward operators who solve real problems rather than those who primarily intermediate them. The organizations that take trucking and logistics to the next level are more likely to be the carriers who innovate under pressure than the larger intermediaries who are structurally slower to adopt and better positioned to crush competition once it appears.

Sources and Bibliography

1. FreightWaves. “Big carriers keep FMCSA’s crackdown alive, Fuller says.” November 7, 2026.

2. Commercial Carrier Journal. “Surprise Motus reclassification threatens small Illinois flatbedder.” October 29, 2026.

3. Commercial Carrier Journal. “FMCSA Motus Registration Portal: Updates, Glitches & Fraud Crackdown.” October 28, 2026.

4. FreightWaves. “FMCSA removes 10,000-plus driver training providers amid safety push.” October 28, 2026.

5. Truck News. “Schneider sees tighter trucking capacity, rising rates and autonomous opportunities ahead.” September 25, 2026.

6. Trucking Dive. “Schneider expects Supreme Court ruling to thin carrier ranks.” October 2026.

7. Commercial Carrier Journal. “FMCSA Crackdowns & CDL Revocations Reshape Trucking Capacity.” October 28, 2026.

8. Trucking Dive. “ATA calls for more English testing, tougher CDL requirements.” October 2025.

9. Overdrive. “Trucking Resurgence: ATA, trucking execs’ plans for non-domiciled CDLs, fraud, more.” December 2025.

10. FMCSA Motus public data dashboard (suspension order counts by month, 2026).

11. Coverage of Knight-Swift statements at industry events, October 2026 (carrier pool reduction of approximately 70 percent).

12. Coverage of C.H. Robinson carrier-base trimming post-Montgomery, 2026.

This analysis draws on contemporaneous reporting from 2025–2026. Figures for non-domiciled CDL removals, English-language proficiency orders, and training-provider removals are those cited by carrier executives and trade publications in October 2026 and are consistent with FMCSA statements during the same period. The carrier-led innovation thesis is presented as an interpretive perspective grounded in the observed dynamics of aligned incentives and organizational structure.

item.title: Risk Doesn't Go Away. It Moves.
item.content:encoded:
⛽ Bigger freight bills don't mean healthier fleets

The numbers: Freight spending rose 20.4% in a year while shipments rose 1.9% (Cass, September). In 2025, refrigerated carriers kept 0.6% and dry van 0.4%, while flatbed and oversize lost 0.5% (ATRI).

  • In the news: Diesel eased to about $6.29 the week of Nov. 2 down from a $6.53 record in September. That is still above the 2022 peak of $5.81.
  • In the news: Tax relief is uneven Indiana's holiday leaves diesel fully taxed and North Dakota operators report limited help .
  • Who really pays: Relief moves the bill. Michigan critics estimate a $600 million hole in road repair money, and one Pennsylvania proposal would draw on the Rainy-Day Fund. When government gives up revenue with no clear way to replace it, the cost tends to return through later taxes, weaker road funding or higher prices overall.

Why it matters: Track profit per mile, not revenue. Reset fuel surcharges often, price each lane on its real cost, and ask your tax adviser whether the deferred federal diesel tax comes due later.

🛡️The insurance market is splitting by fleet quality

  • The numbers: Commercial auto rose 4.5% in Q2 2026 and umbrella rose 5.3%, while premiums across all accounts fell 2% (CIAB).
  • The spread: A USI forecast for the first half of 2026 put fleets under 200 units with good losses at flat to +7.5%. Similar fleets with poor losses were at +20% to +40%.
  • In the news: One trade report says Landstar cut 35,000 carriers and renewed its auto liability flat. Underwriters are paying attention to who you haul with and what you do with your data.

Why it matters: Start your renewal 120 days out. Show what you did with your safety data, not just that you own cameras, and report every driver and truck before the first trip.

⚖️ The cost of a crash is set in the courtroom

  • The numbers : From 2021 to 2024, truck crash rates fell 2.6%, while liability losses per mile rose 33.1% and premiums rose 18.6% (ATRI).
  • In the news: A new U.S. Chamber report, covered by Land Line on Oct. 26, puts the median trucking verdict at $5.2 million and the median settlement at $2.15 million. Average awards were $24.4 million in state courts and $2.1 million in federal courts.
  • The chain got longer: One Ohio Turnpike crash case named 10 defendants, including the toll operator and the shipper. In October, a Texas judge upheld a $604 million verdict against a broker whose carrier held a Satisfactory rating.
  • Who profits: Funded auto injury claims lasted 9.6 times longer and cost 361% more than unfunded ones (Sedgwick). Investors, lobbies and law firms fight over these rules in capitals and courtrooms. A 20-truck fleet rarely has a seat in those rooms, but it still pays through its premium.

Why it matters: Expect brokers and shippers to demand higher limits and tighter contracts. Act on every safety alert and write down what you did, because that record may be read in court.

📋 Paperwork can now park a truck

In the news: As of Nov. 4, DOT reports 33,000 drivers placed out of service over English proficiency and 31,000 CDLs revoked. FMCSA also removed 110 training schools in August.

  • Motus: FMCSA says about 95% of registrations are working and thousands of bad actors have been kept out. The other side: one analysis found 6,475+ carriers suspended, and a small Illinois flatbed carrier told CCJ a surprise reclassification threatens its survival
  • The rules may move again: Pending court cases could revive California's non-domiciled CDL program. CCJ also reports that new Democratic majorities in Congress could push stricter safety mandates and higher insurance minimums in the next highway bill.

Why it matters: A suspended carrier has no revenue. Check your registration record and insurance filings monthly, audit driver files now, and challenge bad data through DataQs.

🚨 Fewer drivers, smarter thieves

  • Drivers : Turnover averaged 44.2% in 2025 (ATRI). Drivers who stayed with one large carrier were about 65% less likely to have a serious crash than drivers who quit. A tight market creates pressure to hire fast, and that is how risk gets in.
  • In the news: FMCSA has proposed removing an online provider that sells two-hour Class A theory courses for $23.
  • In the news: Reported thefts fell 33% in Q3, but losses rose 12% to about $230 million, with fictitious pickups making up about a quarter of incidents Losses through September reached $718.9 million, close to the $725 million estimated for all of2025.
  • In the news: Oakland police are investigating $11.4 million in missing Nvidia hardware, picked up by a truck identified as a food transport company. Criminals are also exploiting established carriers' identities.

Why it matters: One crash can trigger auto, workers' comp and cargo claims at once. Keep your hiring standards when trucks sit and confirm any pickup change by calling a known number.

💳 It all lands on cash, and on who pays

  • The numbers: Allianz Research expects U.S. insolvencies to rise 12% in 2026, to27,700, and keep climbing through 2028. The average freight invoice at one large payment company jumped 30.8% to $2,210.
  • The math:
  • At a 0.6% margin, it takes about $368,000 in new revenue to earn back oneunpaid $2,210 invoice.
  • In the news: FreightWaves counted 16 trucking bankruptcies in under a month in September, then reported 16 more recent cases on Oct. 21. Inc. points to diesel, debt and thin margins.
  • In the news: When brokers including R&R and AGX Freight shut down in early 2026, hundreds of carriers were left chasing money they had already earned. The required broker bond starts at just $75,000.

Why it matters: A trucking company acts like a lender to its customers. Track days-to-pay, know your top three customers' share of revenue, and vet new brokers and shippers before extending terms.

Where trade credit insurance fits: It can protect eligible receivables if a customer becomes insolvent or stays unpaid past the policy's waiting period. It can also support credit decisions and, with a lender's agreement, financing. Terms and exclusions vary by policy.

🗺️Five regions at a glance

The same national pressures look different by region. Diesel figures below are from the week of Oct. 26 (EIA).

Northeast: $6.50 Central Atlantic and $6.42 New England. Highest cost per mile at$2.52, with New York City and Philadelphia on the Judicial Hellholes list. Pennsylvania's diesel tax is 74.1 cents a gallon.

Midwest: $6.48. St. Louis and three Illinois counties are on the Hellholes list, and Illinois is a top three state for cargo theft.

Southeast: $5.89, the lowest region. Florida and Georgia passed major tort reforms, North Carolina banned litigation funding, and storm plans matter.

South Central: $5.95 Gulf Coast. Texas leads truck crash cases with a $20.2 million average, while its private employers may opt out of workers' comp.

West : $7.33 West Coast and $8.16 California. Los Angeles ranks No. 1 on the Hellholes list, and California had 1,218 cargo thefts in 2025.

💡 Final thought

Risk doesn't go away. It moves, and too often it moves to the small fleet that acts as everyone's shock absorber. The fleets that do best price on their real cost, keep a complete file, and know who owes them money and whether that customer can pay. My job is to help you see where the risk is heading before it lands on your balance sheet.

📞 Let's talk

Want the full 2027 U.S. Trucking Risk Outlook? Preparing for a renewal, or worried about a customer who has started paying slower? Message me or call. I'm glad to review your auto, excess, cargo and trade credit exposures with you.

General information only, not legal, tax or financial advice. Coverage depends on actual policy terms.

item.title: Wall Street Is Pricing Your Claims:
item.description: Insurance, Insolvencies and $111 Oil Reset Freight's Risk Math
item.content:encoded:
Landstar and C.H. Robinson posted strong third quarters, and investors still sent their shares sharply lower because of insurance and claims costs. At the same time, small-carrier bankruptcies are piling up, diesel is expected to stay high into 2027, and new research from ATRI and Allianz shows fuel, litigation and insolvency risk at the top of the list. If you own, run or finance a trucking or logistics business, this is the week to look hard at what your risk profile is costing you.

Wall Street Is Now Pricing Claims Risk

• Landstar closed down 17.76% and C.H. Robinson down 11.14% after strong Q3 numbers were overshadowed by insurance. C.H. Robinson's SG&A rose 29.7% "primarily due to higher claims expenses" following the Lipe vs. Lupus Superior verdict and the Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II broker-liability ruling.

• The operating side was strong: C.H. Robinson's North American Surface Transportation operating revenue rose 29.1%, just before its roughly $6B RXO deal, which RXO creator Brad Jacobs publicly backed, arguing brokerage needs scale and density.

• ATRI's 2026 Top Industry Issues survey (3,000+ stakeholders) ranks Lawsuit Abuse Reform #2 and Insurance Cost/Availability #4. ATRI found liability premiums rose 18.2% from 2021–2024 while crash involvement fell 2.6%, with 27%–50% increases for fleets under 100 trucks and a 45% jump in the $10–15M excess layer.

• ATRI also expects Montgomery to push brokers to require much higher carrier limits and to move from contingent to primary coverage.

Why it matters: Claims are no longer a back-office line item; they show up in company value. As brokerage consolidates into fewer, larger players that set carrier insurance and vetting rules, carriers with documented safety and clean loss histories will be the ones that get the freight and the better terms.

Bankruptcies Rising: Your Customers' Credit Is Your Risk

• Small trucking companies have filed 221 bankruptcies in 2026. About two-thirds of surveyed small carriers reported flat or declining revenue as fuel, insurance and financing costs squeezed margins.

• Allianz Research (Oct. 27) projects U.S. business insolvencies up 12% in 2026 to 27,700 cases and rising to 28,800 in 2027, the highest level since 2011. It says fewer than one in two U.S. SMEs is profitable and that a 60% rise in energy costs since January 2026 has cut U.S. Road transportation net margins by about 15 points.

• ATRI puts non-fuel operating costs at a record $1.854 per mile, with 2025 truckload and refrigerated margins below 1%.

• Forward Air kept a "significant portion" of a customer it had said was worth about 10% of revenue (roughly $250M) with a two-year deal, while some business transitions away from November to March. That's a reminder of what customer concentration can do to a P&L.

Why it matters: Allianz warns that a high plateau of insolvencies means extended non-payment and supply-chain disruption risk, and says companies need to monitor key buyers and suppliers. Carrier failures hit shippers and brokers with service and credit losses. Trade credit insurance helps SMEs, 3PLs and freight forwarders protect receivables and keep working capital moving when a customer can't pay.

Fuel Is Trucking's #1 Concern, and Relief Isn't Close

• Brent rose 2% to $111.38 a barrel after Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked a major Saudi refinery. The U.S. also issued its first public advisory since July to avoid unnecessary Hormuz transits.

• AMBEST CEO Chuck Ryan said at the WEX OTR Summit that diesel is unlikely to fall significantly before spring 2027 because of conflicts involving Iran and Russia and constrained U.S. refining and pipeline capacity. ATRI cites the EIA view that diesel would not return to 2025 levels until 2028 at the soonest.

• Fuel Prices are ATRI's #1 industry concern for 2026, up 17 spots, and the first time drivers have ranked fuel as their top issue. ATRI also notes inflation rose 3.4% in August and the Fed raised rates for the first time in three years.

• My take: wars light the match, but persistent inflation is also a vote on fiscal credibility. When government debt keeps climbing without a believable plan to pay for it, prices and rates stay higher for longer, and Allianz expects governments to offer limited fiscal support. Small fleets with thin margins feel that first.

Why it matters: Fuel surcharge gaps and spot lags turn diesel spikes into cash-flow problems. Budget for a range, tighten fuel controls, and watch customers and subcontractors whose working capital is stretched.

Regulators Tighten the Screws: Training, ELDs, CSA and Food Safety

• FMCSA has removed more than 10,000 providers from its Training Provider Registry since December 2025 and more than 100 noncompliant ELDs from its approved list, chief safety officer Steve Dowling said.

• ATRI reports English language proficiency enforcement has placed more than 26,000 drivers out of service since June 2025, and CSA rose to the #3 industry concern, it's highest since 2015, as brokers look for documented proof they hired the safest carriers after Montgomery.

• FDA declared over an E. coli outbreak that sickened 50 people from chicken wraps FSIS confirmed came from Trader Joe's, while a new outbreak is under investigation.

Why it matters: Check that your new hires' training providers and your ELDs are still on FMCSA's lists. Your CSA profile is now a sales document. Food-grade haulers should keep temperature and chain-of-custody records ready in case an investigation reaches their loads.

From Data to Decisions: Telematics That Proves Safety

• ATRI's September 2026 telematics study surveyed 111 motor carriers. More than 90% already use the core safety KPIs: critical events, hard braking, speeding and harsh turning/cornering.

• Maintenance KPIs are the least used category. Nearly half of carriers (48%) don't integrate telematics with maintenance software, 16% don't use a TMS, and 14% of fleets, mostly under 70 trucks, don't use a fleet management system.

• ATRI's truck GPS database captures billions of probe points a year from several hundred thousand large trucks and powers its annual bottleneck analysis of more than 325 locations.

Why it matters: After Montgomery, safety has to be provable. The data most fleets already collect can document safe operations for brokers and underwriters, and ATRI flags preventive maintenance and diagnostics as untapped value. That supports the case for lower total cost of risk.

Ports, Rails and Theft: Southern California Pressure Points

• About 250 ILWU Local 26 watchmen could strike as early as 5 p.m. Pacific on Sunday, Nov. 1. PMA expects other ILWU members to honor picket lines at terminals handling about 85% of Long Beach's and 33% of Los Angeles' cargo.

• 35,688 import containers were awaiting on-dock rail at LA–Long Beach on Oct. 26, with 10,562 waiting nine days or more; dwell for local-truck containers rose to 3.18 days. The September goods trade gap grew 2.1% to $134.9B, the largest since March 2025.

• LAPD traced shoes sold on eBay to a Chatsworth business and recovered 35 pallets of stolen BNSF cargo worth about $1M, after a separate $1M recovery at a Whittier retailer earlier in October.

Why it matters: Congestion and a possible strike mean longer dwell, detention and more time for cargo to sit exposed. Drayage fleets should review cargo, detention and storage exposures now, and shippers waiting on delayed inventory should keep an eye on their own cash flow and their customers' ability to pay.

Capacity Tightens as Equipment Gets Pricier

• Werner CEO Derek Leathers said on Oct. 27 that trucking is entering an upcycle as capacity declines. Old Dominion's September tonnage turned positive for the first time in over two years, with Q3 EPS of $1.65 on $1.59B revenue, but executives said record energy prices must ease for a real upcycle.

• Commerce is imposing tariffs of about 260% on Chinese van-type trailers it says were dumped in the U.S. Paccar's CEO said suppliers couldn't scale as fast as truck demand. Policies framed as protecting domestic producers tend to reward the well-connected incumbents, and fleets buying equipment pay the bill.

• Charger Logistics signed a nonbinding MOU for up to 500 Aurora Driver-powered trucks for 2027–2028 delivery, and Knight-Swift's AAA Cooper LTL network (180 terminals) is eyeing leased terminals in Pennsylvania and Virginia.

Why it matters: Tight capacity can push shippers toward less-vetted carriers, which is exactly the exposure Montgomery created for brokers. Higher trailer and truck prices raise replacement values, so keep physical damage schedules current. Autonomous trucks raise open questions about how liability is shared between fleet and technology provider.

Final Thought

This week made one thing clear: the market now prices risk, not just revenue. Safety and operations lower your total cost of risk. Documented safety data verified hiring and training records, current equipment values, disciplined fuel controls and protected receivables are what separate the companies' investors and underwriters reward from the ones they punish. Insurance is the last line of defense; the best programs start with how you run the business.

Let's Talk

Want to talk through how Montgomery affects your limits, how your claims history is shaping your renewal, or how trade credit insurance could protect your receivables as insolvencies rise? Connect with me here or reach out directly. I'm always glad to share insights, risk management ideas and insurance options that fit your operation.

item.title: Pricing Power Flows Up. Risk Flows Down.
item.content:encoded:
Last week a Texas judge left a broker facing a bill of more than $700 million, the largest truckload carrier told shippers to expect double-digit increases, and diesel turned back up. Each story is about the same thing: who has the power to set the price of risk, and who has to absorb it. For small fleets, brokers, and SMEs that extend terms to bigger customers, that answer decides whether this market is an opportunity or a trap.

A Satisfactory Rating Is No Longer a Defense

• On Oct. 16 a Dallas County judge affirmed the full $604 million verdict against C.H. Robinson in Lipe v. Lupus Superior, plus about $107 million in pre-judgment interest at 6.75%.

• The carrier it hired had a Satisfactory FMCSA rating and had safely delivered nearly 270 of its loads. The jury still found the driver was “subject to control” by the broker.

• The broker's chief legal officer called for “a clear national standard for what constitutes a safe carrier.” A federal carrier-selection bill, H.R. 5337, is still in a House subcommittee.

Why it matters to freight and insurance : When a government rating no longer protects the company that relied on it, the burden of proof moves to the private file, and insurers say they want telematics data, not a broker's word. That is a fixed cost that big fleets spread across thousands of trucks, and a 10-truck fleet carries alone. Watch who writes any national standard: whoever defines “safe” also decides whose compliance is cheap and whose is expensive. Small carriers need a seat at that table, and a complete file in the meantime.

Fuel Is a Loan You Make to Your Customer

• EIA's benchmark diesel rose 9.7 cents to $6.276 a gallon for the week of Oct. 19, the first increase in four weeks and $2.66 above a year ago.

• ATRI's annual survey of nearly 3,100 respondents ranked fuel trucking's No. 1 concern, up 17 spots, and put operating cost per mile excluding fuel at $1.85, the highest in 18 years of its research.

• The California Trucking Association says fuel surcharges cover only about 70% to 75% of fuel cost for many small carriers. EIA cautioned diesel may not return to 2025 levels until at least 2028.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: A small carrier pays at the pump today and collects 30 or more days later, so every gallon is credit extended to the shipper. Higher fuel also feeds the general price level: ATRI's report notes inflation ran 3.4% in August and the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years, which makes that credit more expensive to carry. And the deferred 24.4-cent dyed-diesel tax still has no payment rule, so some of today's fuel cost is simply a bill postponed. Price on real cost and reserve for what is deferred.

Scale Reprices. Small Fleets Wait.

• Knight-Swift's third-quarter revenue rose 14.2% to $2.2 billion and operating income rose 255% to$178.7 million. Truckload revenue per loaded mile, excluding fuel, rose 9.7%.

• It ran about 4% fewer tractors than a year ago, and its rate gains outpaced cost inflation by 840 basis points, according to FreightWaves.

• CEO Adam Miller said 2027 bids will open at “probably low to mid double digits,” adding that the market's challenges “have not been demand driven. It's been more capacity driven.”

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Rates are high because trucks are being removed from the market, not because freight is booming. That is a price signal created by supply restrictions, and the companies with scale and pricing power capture it first. Leased-on owner-operators' median earnings fell to just over $170,000 in 2025 from $186,016 in 2023, per ATA (with different samples). Capital that treats this as a demand boom will be misallocated. For anyone extending terms, bigger invoices from the same customers mean bigger receivables at risk.

Fewer, Bigger Doors

• C.H. Robinson agreed to buy RXO for an enterprise value of $5.8 billion. Insurance Business says the combined broker would be more than twice the size of its next competitor.

• A Higginbotham transportation leader said much of the selling comes from tight margins and owner fatigue, and that large buyers often self-insure a primary layer a typical trucking company has to buy.

• About 25,000 Mexican freight drivers have lost U.S. visas, per C.H. Robinson's October report, and Werner's CEO publicly backed tougher cabotage, B-1 visa, and English-proficiency enforcement.

Why it matters to freight and insurance : Tougher enforcement may well be sound safety policy. It also shrinks supply, which raises rates for the carriers that remain, so the largest incumbents have every incentive to support it. Add consolidation and self-insurance, and the advantages of scale compound: the big can wait, negotiate, and absorb, while small carriers and brokers face fewer customers, higher fixed costs, and more concentrated credit exposure to whichever giant owes them money.

Failure Travels Down the Chain

• FreightWaves counted at least 16 carriers filing bankruptcy between Sept. 18 and Oct. 21, from one-truck operators to a 53-truck logging fleet.

• In Oregon, Eskil Trucking's largest creditor claim, nearly $855,000, is owed to another trucking company, Sargent Transportation.

• A New Orleans attorney got 32 months in federal prison for his role in 31 staged tractor-trailer crashes; the kind of fraud that inflates the severity every fleet pays for in premium.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: The Eskil case says it plainly: in trucking, your biggest credit risk is often another trucking company . When a customer fails, the loss lands on whoever extended terms, and no rate increase recovers an invoice that will never be paid. Trade credit insurance exists for exactly this, protecting receivables against a customer's insolvency or protracted default so one failure down the chain does not become yours.

Final Thought

My job is to read the market the way an underwriter does: follow the cost until you find who is actually holding it. This week the answer kept coming back the same. Liability moved to whoever picked the carrier, fuel cost moved to whoever waits to be paid, and pricing power moved to whoever has the scale to wait. When the rules, the rates, and the relief are shaped most by those with the most access, small businesses become everyone else's shock absorber, and that weakens both fair competition and the shared prosperity built on it. Honest pricing, real cash reserves, a complete file, and protected receivables are how an SME stops carrying someone else's risk.

Let's Talk

If you want to pressure-test your carrier file, your fuel exposure, or the receivables you are carrying for larger customers the way an underwriter would, reach out. I'm glad to share insights, risk management advice, and insurance solutions, including trade credit insurance for SMEs.

item.title: Who Referees the Claim? The Case for an Independent Claims Review
item.content:encoded:
📊 The Scorecard Problem: What Counts as a "Win"?

  • In an Oct 22 post, coverage attorney Chip Merlin looks at internal State Farm claim-quality documents from an Oklahoma bad faith case. A June 2021 report listed fewer full roof replacements, fewer wind/hail estimates over $10,000 (down 13% year over year) and more claims closed without payment as "quality indicators trending positively."
  • In his view, a lower payment isn't proof of better adjusting, and neither is a higher one. The real test is whether the policyholder got everything owed after a fair investigation. State Farm disputes the allegations, and the release of the documents is not a finding of bad faith.
  • Trucking tie-in: Fleets face the same metrics on cargo, physical damage and liability files. When claim teams are scored on spending, an independent check shows whether a decision followed the facts or the dashboard.

🤖 "Touchless Claims" and Outcome-Based Handling

  • NonDoc reports that the same unsealed documents describe a plan to automate claims, including goals of handling 35-40% of claims with no human involvement and doing 40% of damage evaluations virtually. The documents also describe "outcome-based claim handling."
  • The plaintiffs' attorneys argue this violates Oklahoma's good-faith duty and point to projected savings of $218-300 million. State Farm did not respond to NonDoc. These are claims made in active litigation.
  • Trucking tie-in: Photo-only estimates on a damaged tractor or reefer unit can miss frame and electrical damage. When a model makes the decision, someone independent should be able to look at what it got wrong.

⚖️ Washington Writes Transparency into the Rules

  • According to Wood, Smith, Henning & Berman, Washington's amended claims regulations took effect Oct 18, 2026. Under the new rules, an investigation can't rely solely on a database or estimating software, and insureds can ask for their claim file before filing suit.
  • For auto claims, insurers can't require photo-only evaluations. They must offer an in-person inspection and complete one within five business days if a virtual inspection leads to a dispute
  • Trucking tie-in: This is what part of an independent process looks like in practice: open files, disclosed pricing data and a human inspection on request. Rules like these tend to spread from state to state.

🧠 AI Oversight Becomes the Regulatory Norm

  • Cozen O'Connor's October Claims Notes reports that 29 jurisdictions have adopted the NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI. California, Colorado, New York and Texas have issued their own guidance.
  • The bulletin holds insurers accountable for decisions made by AI, including in claims handling.
  • Trucking tie-in: Governance makes it possible to audit how a claim was decided. The next step is a review that someone outside the carrier can trust.

🚛 Trucking Verdicts Nearly Quadruple, and Claim Costs Outrun Rates

  • Transport Topics covered a forthcoming U.S. Chamber ILR study of 334 trucking verdicts and settlements. The median verdict rose from $760,000 in 2023 to $3 million in 2026, and the median settlement rose from $210,000 to $2.2 million. FedEx's claims counsel pointed to fraud networks, including staged crashes.
  • Insurance Business reports that AM Best found first-year commercial auto liability loss payments grew 6.4% a year from 2014 to 2024, compared with 2.8% general inflation.
  • Bigger picture: When government spending and debt keep pushing up prices, repair costs, medical bills and reserves rise with them. Who gets heard when tort and claims rules are written matters as much as the rates themselves.
  • Trucking tie-in: Settlements between $500K and $5M can land inside deductibles and SIRs. An independent review of reserves and settlement decisions protects the fleet that's paying part of the bill.

🔍 What an Independent Claims Review Could Look Like (My Perspective)

  • A neutral reviewer: a licensed, independent adjuster or panel reviews disputed or large files and has no incentive tied to the size of the payment.
  • Transparent metrics: measure accuracy, including missed damage and underpayments, not just savings and claims closed without payment.
  • Documented decisions: every manager or model override is written down with the claim-specific evidence behind it and shared with the insured.
  • Appraisal/umpire mechanics : many properties and auto physical damage policies already have appraisal clauses, where each side picks an appraiser and an umpire settles disagreements. A similar structure could work more broadly.
  • Existing analogs to build on : independent adjusters, state insurance department complaint processes, and claim-file access rules like Washington's new regulation.
  • This is my view on how the industry could do better, not legal advice. Check your policy wording and talk to counsel about specific disputes.

💡 Final Thought

Insurance works when people trust it. Insureds need to know they were paid what they were owed, carriers need to know they weren't overcharged, and agents need to stand behind both. An independent claims process between the client and the carrier gives everyone that confidence. Until the industry builds one, my job is to fill that role for you: document the file, challenge the numbers and make sure the right decision gets made.

Want help reviewing a claim, your loss runs, or your fleet's overall risk program? Reach out.

Sources

1. State Farm's Claims Scorecard: What Does Management Call a Win? (Property Insurance Coverage Law Blog, Oct 22, 2026): https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/blog/statefarm-claims-scorecard-quality-metrics/

2. 'Touchless claims': State Farm documents reveal intent to automate claims process with AI (NonDoc, Oct 1, 2026): https://nondoc.com/2026/10/01/touchless-claims-state-farm-documentsreveal-intent-to-automate-claims-process-with-ai/

3. Washington's Claims-Handling Regulations are Changing on October 18, 2026 (Wood, Smith, Henning & Berman): https://www.wshblaw.com/experience-washingtons-claims-handlingregulations-are-changing-on-october-18-2026

4. Claims Notes: October 2026 (Cozen O'Connor, Oct 19, 2026): https://www.cozen.com/newsresources/publications/2026/claims-notes-october-2026

5. Size of trucking verdicts quadruples over 2023-2026 time span (Transport Topics, Oct 19, 2026): https://www.ttnews.com/articles/trucking-verdicts-quadruples

6. Litigation costs keep outpacing commercial auto rate increases (Insurance Business, Oct 19, 2026): https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/auto-motor/litigation-costs-keepoutpacing-commercial-auto-rate-increases-594067.aspx

item.title: Fuel Took the Top Spot. Liability Is Where the Long-Term Cost Lives.
item.content:encoded:
The American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI) released its Critical Issues in the Trucking Industry – 2026 report this month. More than 3,000 stakeholders ranked their top concerns between August 24 and October 2, 2026. The mix: motor carrier executives and personnel (48.5%), professional drivers (25.8%) and others including suppliers, driver trainers and law enforcement (25.7%). The headline is fuel. The more durable story, in my view, is how tightly the next several issues are linked. I read the list through one question: where does the risk land, and who ends up paying for it?

Fuel: The Most Visible Pressure, Not the Only One

Fuel Prices rose 17 spots to #1. That's only the fourth time in the survey's 22-year history it has topped the list, after 2005, 2008 and 2022. The report ties the spike to disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. It also cites the EIA's caution that diesel may not return to 2025 levels until 2028 at the soonest. ATRI's cost research put truckload and refrigerated operating margins below 1% in 2025. At margins that thin, fuel surcharge gaps and spot-market lag go straight to cash flow. ATRI notes the pressure falls hardest on small and mid-size fleets.

Litigation: Now the Top Concern for Carriers Themselves

Across all respondents, Lawsuit Abuse Reform held at #2. Among motor carrier respondents, it's now #1. ATRI's litigation research finds the most expensive half of awards growing 5.7% per year. Non-economic and punitive damages average 84% of nuclear verdict totals. In seven states, median nuclear verdicts against the industry ranged from $13.2 million to $213.2 million. There's movement. The report says eight states passed third-party litigation measures in 2026, and North Carolina became the first to ban third-party litigation investment outright. Because reform is uneven, a fleet's exposure is shaped by where its trucks run as much as by how they're driven.

CSA: From Compliance Metric to Vetting Document

CSA climbed to #3, its highest ranking since 2015. ATRI attributes this largely to the May 14, 2026, Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport. As the report describes it, the Court held that freight brokers can be found liable for negligent hiring when a contracted carrier is involved in a crash. ATRI's read is that brokers will need documented evidence they selected safe carriers, and CSA scores are one form of that documentation. That makes CSA a commercial issue as much as a regulatory one. Two details matter here. First, enforcement varies by geography. A 2014 ATRI study found that normalizing state enforcement disparities would move individual carrier scores anywhere from a 17.7-point decrease to a 12.2-point increase. Second, FMCSA has planned changes: reorganized compliance categories, simplified severity weights and more weight on recent violations. They're worth modeling against your own data before they take effect.

Insurance: Where the Other Issues Converge

Insurance Cost / Availability sits at #4. ATRI found motor carrier liability premiums rose 18.2% from 2021 to 2024, while industry crash involvement fell 2.6%. For fleets with fewer than 100 trucks, increases ran 27% to 50% over those four years. Coverage in the $10–15 million excess layer rose 45%. ATRI expects Montgomery to push rates higher for carriers and brokers alike. It also expects brokers to contractually require much higher carrier limits. The top strategy respondents chose (41.1%) was a framework for upfront premium reductions when carriers adopt proven safety technologies. That tells me carriers want safety investment recognized now, not years later when it finally shows up in loss history.

Drivers and a Supply-Side Recovery

Driver Shortage returned at #5 and Driver Retention at #10. ATRI characterizes the freight recovery as supply-driven rather than demand-driven. Carriers reduced effective capacity by 5.5% in 2025 and trimmed driver workforces by 6.4%. English language proficiency enforcement has placed more than 26,000 drivers out of service since June 2025 (per U.S. DOT), and more than 100 CDL schools have been shut down. ATRI's cost data tie each additional 30 minutes of average dwell time per stop to a 5.4-point increase in turnover. Each additional $5,000 in average annual pay goes with a 2.9-point improvement. Turnover isn't only an HR metric. Every replacement hire is a new qualification file, a new training gap and a period of elevated exposure.

AI: Tool and Threat

AI in Trucking rose three spots to #7. The report credits AI with safety and productivity gains, such as camera-based coaching and predictive maintenance. It also notes AI is making cargo theft harder to deter. ATRI is candid that it's still uncertain which use cases will become standard and which will be seen as expensive experiments.

Final Thought

Read as a list, these are ten separate concerns. Read as a risk picture, they connect: fuel compresses margin, litigation trends drive liability and excess costs, Montgomery turns CSA data into a commercial credential and driver churn feeds the exposure underwriters price. My read is that the fleets best positioned for 2027 will treat safety data, driver retention and contract terms as one total-cost-of-risk discussion, not as separate budget lines.

Source: American Transportation Research Institute, Critical Issues in the Trucking Industry – 2026 (October 2026).

Michael Havemeyer, TRS, TCS
Michael.Havemeyer@highstreetins.com | 484-960-9231

item.title: Motus, phishing and the price of "affordable": where this week's risk landed 🚛
item.content:encoded:
🚛 Motus: When the Registry Becomes the Risk

FMCSA moved carrier registration to its new Motus system in May. On October 1, FMCSA Deputy Administrator Jesse Elison told an industry conference that the weeks after launch “were really really tough” and that the system “is not where it needs to be,” while forecasting front-end fixes in “weeks” (FreightWaves).

• Suspended with insurance in force . Fusable’s CAB counted more than 1,200 carriers under an “involuntary suspension” for insurance reasons even though they had active filings meeting their minimums. FMCSA has been restoring authorities one case at a time (Overdrive, Sept.).

• Wrong limits on the record. A Cottingham & Butler safety consultant said Motus showed some carriers needing $5 million in coverage when their actual requirement was $1 million, or in some cases $750,000 (Overdrive, Oct. 13).

• No one answers . Overdrive’s Oct. 13 roundup quotes a compliance consultant on hold for seven hours and 47 minutes before the call dropped. In a public carrier support group I reviewed, members describe 3-to-5-hour holds and authorities “pending” for months. Those are members’ own reports, not verified findings.

• Class actions: talk, but no filing found . Carriers in forums and support groups are calling for a class action. As of October 16, I could not find one that had actually been filed. FMCSA and OOIDA are resolving cases individually. Whether claims against a federal agency can succeed is a question for attorneys.

• Some relief. FMCSA has temporarily suspended biennial-update enforcement, and the DOT-number inactivation's that go with it, for registrants whose update was due on or after June 1, 2026.

Why it matters for trucking, logistics and insurance: brokers vet carriers on federal records, so a wrong status means lost loads through no fault of the carrier. Insurers may not reinstate without active authority, and only your insurer or filing agent can refile the BMC-91/91X.

Do this now: screenshot your status on Motus and SAFER with the date showing • confirm your BIPD filing, BOC-3 and MCS-150 • open a case at 1-800-832-5660 and log the number • send proof to brokers, shippers and your insurer • escalate to the FMCSA PA Division (717-614-4060), PMTA or your U.S. Representative.

Scam alert: fake “New MOTUS Portal” emails are circulating. The only real site is motus.dot.gov . Type it in yourself.

Brokers, shippers and factors: a customer stuck in authority limbo can’t invoice, and a customer that

🎣 Your next stolen load may start in your inbox

Load theft today often starts with a convincing email or a phone call, not a bolt cutter. Someone poses as you, your customer or your vendor, and the freight or the payment goes somewhere it shouldn’t.

• Trucking is a target. The IBM X-Force Threat Intelligence Index 2026 ranks transportation as the fifth most attacked industry in 2025. A Marsh Agency trucking brief says cyber-related load diversion was tied to $725 million in U.S. and Canadian losses in 2025, and cites FBI IC3 figures of $274,000 lost per stolen shipment, on average.

• IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 : the global average breach hit a record $4.99 million (up 12%), and the U.S. average reached $11.5 million. In transportation the average was $4.50 million, up from $3.98 million. Phishing was the top way in for the fourth straight year, and voice and text-message phishing led to the costliest breaches, at $5.29 million.

• Slow is expensive. Breaches that took more than 200 days to find and contain averaged $5.65 million, versus $4.32 million for faster ones. Only 42% of organizations had fully recovered, and fewer than 1 in 20 recovered in under 50 days.

• Margin math (modeled illustration, not a source statistic): at a 10% margin, putting $500 in the bank takes $5,000 in sales. Replacing one $274,000 stolen load would take about $2.74 million in revenue.

Do this Monday: (1) confirm every payment, banking or load change by calling a number already on file • (2) turn on multi-factor authentication for email, banking, load boards, factoring and ELD/fleet systems • (3) split who sets up a vendor from who approves bank changes • (4) vet first-time carriers, brokers and last-minute changes • (5) test your backups and hold a 15-minute scam huddle.

Insurance tie-in: ask your agent whether your policies respond to social engineering and funds-transfer fraud, and how your cargo coverage treats freight released to an impostor . Most of the fix is process; the insurance question is what’s left over when the process fails.

📉 Why "affordable" can cost more

Two pieces I read this week from a Stanford economist ask why price caps and subsidies are so popular when they keep failing. Here’s how I’d frame them for people who move freight and manage risk. The trucking applications are my reading, not the author’s.

• The bill doesn’t disappear . It moves. The essay cites a Wall Street Journal poll showing broad, bipartisan support for capping credit card rates at 10% (78%, 83% and 76% of Democrats, Republicans and independents) and for capping rent increases (65% overall). His core point is that government can’t make things cheaper overall by taxing, spending, borrowing or regulating. It can only shift who pays.

• Borrowed relief comes back as higher prices . My read for our industry: when relief is paid for with borrowing and nobody plans to cover it with future taxes or spending cuts, the cost tends to come back across the economy as a higher price level, in diesel, parts, repair labor and medical bills. Those are the same inputs that drive claim costs, and they eventually show up at renewal.

• Caps ration . The essay notes that price controls have led to rationing and black markets wherever they’ve been tried. A 10% card cap sounds like relief for a small carrier running fuel on plastic. In practice, lenders tend to respond by cutting off the thinnest credit files first. Mandates work the same way: tell insurers to cover more and, as the author puts it, they “just raise premiums.”

• Follow the organized interest s. His list of policies that raise costs reads like a freight bill: ethanol requirements (he estimates about 30 cents a gallon on diesel), the Jones Act, tariffs, limits on automated ports, and occupational licensing. Each has an organized, well-connected group that benefits, while the cost is spread thinly across everyone who moves goods. It’s the same pattern as Motus: the players with staff, capital and access get through, and the small operator waits.

Why it matters for trucking, logistics and insurance: plan for cost inflation in your coverage, not just your budget. Check that equipment values, cargo limits and business-income coverage reflect today’s replacement costs. Stress-test receivables from customers who would be squeezed by tighter credit, and consider trade credit insurance for receivables you can’t afford to lose.

💡 Final Thought

This week’s three stories share a thread. When a system fails, whether it’s a federal database, an email inbox or a well-meant policy, the cost lands on whoever has the least cushion. My job is to help you see where that cost would land in your business before it does, and to make sure your insurance and your processes are built for it.

Let’s Talk 📞

If you want a second set of eyes on your Motus filings, your cyber and cargo coverage, or the credit risk sitting in your receivables, reply or call me. I’m an insurance agent with Highstreet, and I’m glad to walk through it with you.

Sources: FreightWaves, “FMCSA’s Elison: ‘weeks’ away from fixing Motus user experience” (Oct. 1, 2026); Overdrive, “FMCSA’s Motus mess costing small fleets thousands,” “FMCSA cleaning up Motus mess one carrier at a time” (Sept. 2026) and “FMCSA’s Motus mess improving, little by little?” (Oct. 13, 2026); FMCSA, Temporary Suspension of the Biennial Update Requirement; Highstreet Motus help sheet (Oct. 2026); review of a public carrier Motus support group (member reports, unverified); IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 (Ponemon Institute); IBM X-Force Threat Intelligence Index 2026; Marsh Agency, “Trucking through cyber risk” (2026, citing FBI IC3); two Oct. 13–14, 2026 essays on affordability published on Substack, which cite a Wall Street Journal poll. Margin math is a modeled illustration. This is general information, not legal advice. Coverage depends on actual policy terms.

item.title: Capacity Left the Market. The Risk Didn't Leave With It.
item.content:encoded:
Freight prices are climbing, but the freight itself is not. This week's headlines on diesel, court rulings, fraud, and bankruptcies are really one story: when relief is deferred, rules are written by the biggest players, and credit is stretched to cover the gap, the cost lands on the small business that extends terms. For trucking, logistics, and insurance leaders, the question is not where rates go next, but who is protected when payment slows down.

Freight Prices Are Rising Without More Freight

• Carriers are rejecting about four times as many load tenders as in October 2023, yet volume is up only about 9%. For-hire tractors fell roughly 51,000 in a single month.

• Contract dry van linehaul now runs 22 cents a mile above spot ($2.39 vs. $2.17 in August), and the September Logistics Managers' Index showed a tenth straight month of shrinking capacity.

• Rates are being set by what has left the market, not by what shippers want to move. Each load now carries more dollars, and so more exposure, per invoice.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Higher prices on the same freight mean larger receivables on every load. For a small carrier, broker, or 3PL, one unpaid invoice now does more damage than it did a year ago. When prices rise on supply and cost instead of demand, the pressure lands on whoever is extending credit.

Diesel Is a Tax on Time

• Diesel sits near $6.28 a gallon, about $2.60 above last year, with a hurricane over Gulf refining capacity. Fleets pay for fuel today and collect weeks later.

• The new dyed-diesel order defers the 24-cent federal tax rather A deferral is not relief. It moves the bill to a later date and a different balance sheet, and every waiver, holiday, and exemption has to be paid for by someone.

• State tax holidays are a patchwork, and a Texas fuel waiver comes with engine-warranty warnings for newer trucks.

Why it matters to freight and insurance : Fuel is a working-capital problem before it is a margin problem. Every cent of tax that is deferred instead of cut is a debt someone will eventually fund, and the cost of that tends to show up later in prices. Patchwork relief also distorts the signals that tell a carrier what a mile really costs, so capital goes to the wrong places. Honest cost accounting and credit discipline beat borrowed time. Trade credit insurance and supply chain finance keep cash moving while those timing gaps open.

The Carrier File Is the Product

• After the Montgomery ruling, a broker's vetting record is what courts, insurers, and plaintiffs examine. One large agency just made transportation a full division for that reason.

• This week's cases show why paper is not protection. A jury convicted two men who bought real trucking companies to steal loads, and another man was sentenced for a $3.5 million Amazon Relay fraud across 23 fake accounts.

• Reporters also found ELD vendors that admitted to selling hours-of-service cheating, and the paper medical card waiver ends October 11.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Clean-looking authority, CSA scores, and a registered ELD are no longer enough on their own. Ownership changes, identity checks, and driver qualification records are what hold up in a deposition, and what underwriters now price. Who sets the standard also matters. Broker trade groups are lobbying Washington for a federal carrier-selection rule while courts write one case by case. When the rules are shaped by the parties with the most access, the cost of compliance falls hardest on the smallest fleets.

Bigger Buyers, Thinner Carriers

• C.H. Robinson agreed to buy RXO for $5.8 billion, creating a more concentrated buyer of truckload capacity.

• At the other end, at least 16 trucking companies filed for bankruptcy between late August and September 21, and Chicago's Midwest Expedited followed on October 6 with $2.3 million in liabilities.

• Fuel cards are now being bundled with factoring for fleets under 21 trucks, tying a small carrier's fuel, cash flow, and credit risk to one provider.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Scale is becoming a credit credential, and size increasingly decides who gets paid on time and who gets squeezed. A market where the largest buyers consolidate, set the terms, and have the most access to the people writing the rules is a stacked deck, and it weakens both competition and the broad prosperity that depends on it. When a carrier fails, the risk does not disappear. It relocates to factors, brokers with loads in transit, and insurers with unpaid premium. SMEs that sell to larger buyers need protection against that shift in who holds the cash.

Severity Is Being Engineered

• Nuclear verdicts rose 41% in 2025, and U.S. litigation funding tops $16 billion a year. Plaintiff firms now use data, online mock juries, and AI to push verdicts higher.

• In the Permian Basin, the deadliest truck corridor has a fatal crash rate about 8.8 times the Texas average, and a single $49 million verdict came from the same area.

• Excess liability layers are up 34% to 45%, which means the limits that protect a balance sheet cost far more.

Why it matters to freight and insurance: Insurance is moving from pricing fleets to pricing lanes, hiring files, and documentation. Rising severity is not random. It is built on organized capital and sophisticated process, and it drains the same cash that carriers need for fuel and payroll. The best defense is a file that holds up and balance-sheet protection that does not depend on every customer paying.

Final Thought

Every week, the market gives the same lesson in a different form: risk does not go away, it moves, and when the deck is stacked toward the best-connected, it moves downhill to the businesses with the least say in the rules. That erodes more than margins. It erodes the trust in fair markets and accountable government that real prosperity rests on. It moves from the carrier to the broker, from the fuel pump to the receivable, from the courtroom to the premium. The companies that stay tendered and stay paid are the ones that know where the risk has landed, document it, and protect the cash behind it. Protection is not the opposite of growth. It is what makes growth survivable.

Let's Talk

If you want to walk through your carrier-selection file, your fuel and payment terms, or your open-account exposure the way an underwriter or a plaintiff's lawyer would, reach out. I'm glad to share insights, risk management advice, and insurance solutions, including trade credit insurance for SMEs.
