item.title: The First Carriers to Fail Aren't Unsafe. They're Out of Cash.
item.content:encoded:
ATRI’s 2023 operational-cost update, covering 2022, put the average marginal cost of running a truck at $2.251 a mile and $90.78 an hour, the first time the series cleared $2 a mile. Fuel was $0.641 of that, up 53.7 percent from $0.417, and its share of marginal cost rose from 22 percent to 28 percent. Strip fuel out and costs still rose 12 percent. Driver wages were up 15.5 percent, truck and trailer payments 18.6 percent, repair and maintenance 12 percent.

That year was the spike everyone remembers. The freight recession that followed took the rate and left the cost. ATRI’s 2024 critical-issues survey found rates still slipping, tonnage below 2023, insurance up 12.5 percent in 2023 and still rising, truck-transportation employment down 2.7 percent from January 2023 to September 2024, and the count of registered carriers in steady decline. Diesel had eased to $3.54 by late September 2024, which is why fuel fell from the number one issue in 2022 to number 11. Owner-operators still ranked it fifth. They were reading their own settlement, not the national average.

The September 2026 telematics report picks up the other half of the squeeze. Costs excluding fuel are up 39 percent since 2020. Freight volumes are essentially unchanged since 2023. ATA tonnage fell another 1 percent in July 2026. Deadhead, dwell, and miles between breakdowns have worsened under that pressure. Fuel use and miles per gallon are among the highest-value operating metrics carrier's track. Cost per mile is rated just as important and is one of the clearest adoption gaps. Fleets that cannot see cost per mile in something close to real time are managing a diesel market they cannot measure.

Why the small carrier exits first

Fleets with 10 or fewer trucks are 95.7 percent of carriers registered with U.S. DOT. They do not have the tools the large fleets use to mute a diesel move.

In the 2022 data, truckload fleets with fewer than 26 trucks spent 19.5 percent more per mile on fuel than truckload fleets with more than 1,000 trucks. Specialized fleets under 26 trucks spent 24.9 percent more. Large carriers hedge, buy in bulk, and negotiate card discounts. A one-truck operation buys retail, one fill at a time, on a lane it cannot reroute.

Operating results split the same way. Across sectors, fleets under 26 trucks saw average operating margin fall from 13.5 percent to 9.3 percent as the spot market cooled. Fleets over 1,000 trucks improved, to 13.1 percent. Truckload margins fell from 10 percent to 8 percent, flatbed from 10 percent to 7 percent, refrigerated from 11 percent to 6 percent. Fuel surcharges explained most of the revenue-per-mile increase that year. Surcharges lag the pump, and on a short-haul or brokered load they often do not cover the fill that got the truck to the shipper.

At $6.38, a truck at 6.5 miles per gallon burns about 98 cents a mile in fuel before DEF, idle, or out-of-route miles. That is more than half a typical truckload marginal-cost stack from the last full ATRI cost year, and it is cash. The broker still pays in 30 to 60 days.

The cash-conversion tax

This is where diesel stops being an operating expense and becomes a financing problem.

A fuel advance, whether from the broker or the factor, usually releases 30 to 50 percent of the load at pickup. It is not extra money. It is an early slice of the same invoice, deducted from settlement. Broker advances often carry a $5 to $25 flat fee or 1 to 3 percent. If the advance arrives as an EFS money code or check, the truck stop commonly charges about 3 percent to cash it, often waived only if the driver buys 25 gallons or more on the spot. A $500 code at 3 percent is $15 gone before the truck is fueled, and the fuel is bought at the counter price.

An EFS fuel card is a different product. In-network, the driver pays the cash price rather than the credit price, plus a negotiated discount that in practice often lands around $0.05 to $0.15 a gallon. On a 150-gallon fill at $6.38, ten cents is $15. Useful, and nowhere near the move from $3.75 to $6.38. Factoring the invoice after delivery still costs 1.5 to 5 percent of the load, most small carriers nearer 2 to 3.5 percent. Recourse factoring leaves the carrier holding the invoice if the broker does not pay.

Stack it. A $2,000 load, a $15 advance fee, a waived cashing fee, a 3 percent factoring fee, and fuel at 98 cents a mile for 500 miles. Fuel is $490. Factoring is $60. The advance fee is $15. More than a quarter of the load is gone before the truck payment, insurance, and the driver’s draw. The large fleet paid less per gallon, billed a fuel surcharge on a contract, and did not sell the invoice to make payroll.

Insurance is the second exit ramp. ATRI’s 2024 survey ranked insurance cost and availability fourth among carriers. A carrier already late on a premium, or coming up on renewal after a nuclear-verdict year, does not get to shop its way out of a $6 diesel market. The authority goes dormant. The truck parks. The capacity that leaves is the capacity that was never in a large fleet’s network.

What resilience looks like before the authority goes dormant

For the one-truck and small-fleet operator, the lever is not a better forecast of crude. It is shrinking the cash gap and the gallons.

• Price the lane with fuel as a cash item, not a surcharge footnote. If the DOE index the contract uses is a week behind a 30-cent move, the shortfall is the carriers.

• Take the advance on the card or by ACH, not as a code that has to be cashed. The discount is on the card. The fee is on the code.

• Do not stack a broker advance on top of a factoring advance. One fee is a tool. Two fees are a rate cut.

• Treat miles per gallon as a survival metric. ATRI’s telematics work ties fuel waste directly to speeding, hard braking, and idle. A half mile-per-gallon improvement on 100,000 miles is real money at this pump price, and it does not require a new truck.

• Know the renewal date on liability and cargo. A diesel spike and a non-renewal in the same month is how authorities exit.

For the broker, shipper, and insurer, the signal is not the national average. It is the share of a lane sitting on carriers with fewer than 10 trucks, paid on spot, fueling at retail, and factoring every invoice. That capacity is the first to fail a credit check, miss a pickup, or file a claim because the truck was running a cheap tire and a late PM. ATRI’s 2026 telematics survey found maintenance metrics highly valued and thinly used, and larger fleets far more likely to have the systems that produce them. The small carrier’s breakdown becomes the shipper’s missed window and the insurer’s loss run.

Diesel at $6.38 does not have to stay there to do the damage. It has to stay above the rate long enough that the carrier with no reserve cannot make the next fill. That process is already in the carrier-count data from the last freight recession. This pump price accelerates it.

Sources in the draft are ATRI’s Operational Costs of Trucking: 2023 Update, Critical Issues in the Trucking Industry – 2024, and From Data to Decisions (September 2026), plus the EIA weekly diesel series. I left the Kansas City Fed immigration note out. It explains wage cooling in 2022–23, not this diesel moves.

Michael Havemeyer, TRS, TCS
Michael.Havemeyer@highstreetins.com | 484-960-9231

item.title: Non-Recourse Factoring vs. Trade Credit Insurance: What's the Difference?
item.content:encoded:
Factors are the moral equivalent of a loan shark. A lot of trucking companies will hear the term "non-recourse factoring" and assume it provides the same protection; it doesn’t. What it does is charge you a fee many times greater than TCI policy without the advantages of trade credit insurance. It’s a bad deal.

A Simple Example

Imagine you sold lemonade and let your customer pay later.

Recourse factoring: A factor advances you cash today. If your customer never pays, the factor can charge the invoice back to you. You paid a fee, but you still own the risk.

Non-recourse factoring: A factor advances you cash today. If the customer goes bankrupt and the loss meets the contract's requirements, the factor absorbs the loss. You keep the cash, but you pay a higher fee for that protection.

The key detail is that most non-recourse programs only cover a narrow set of credit events, typically bankruptcy or insolvency.

They generally do not protect you if:

  • The broker disputes the load
  • The customer claims service issues
  • Paperwork is incomplete or submitted late
  • The customer is simply slow to pay
  • There is a short-pay or collection dispute

In trucking, these situations account for a large portion of unpaid invoice problems.

Comparing the Three Solutions

Recourse Factoring

  • Provides immediate cash flow
  • Factor advances funds against invoices
  • You remain responsible for unpaid invoices
  • Customer is typically notified
  • Typical cost: ~1.5% to 3.5% per invoice

Non-Recourse Factoring

  • Provides immediate cash flow
  • Covers certain approved credit losses
  • Usually only covers bankruptcy or insolvency
  • Operational disputes still come back to you
  • Customer is typically notified
  • Typical cost: ~3% to 5% per invoice

Trade Credit Insurance (TCI)

  • Does not purchase your invoices
  • Remains invisible to your customers
  • Monitors buyer credit quality year-round
  • Typically covers insolvency and extended non-payment (subject to policy terms)
  • Let’s you keep control of collections and customer relationships
  • Can support lower-cost bank financing
  • Typical cost: roughly 0.15% to 0.30% of insured annual sales

Why the Confusion?

Both non-recourse factoring and trade credit insurance can respond when a customer becomes insolvent. That's where the similarity largely ends.

A non-recourse factor:

  • Buys the invoice
  • Advances 80% to 95% of its value
  • Handles collections
  • Covers some losses on approved debtors
  • Still leaves many operational disputes with you

Trade Credit Insurance:

  • Does not buy the invoice
  • Stays in the background
  • Continuously monitors buyer risk
  • Provides insurance protection for covered losses
  • Helps preserve customer relationships
  • Can be paired with a bank line for lower-cost working capital

Three Questions to Ask Any "Non-Recourse" Factor

  1. Is coverage limited to bankruptcy, or does it also cover extended non-payment?
  2. What happens if the broker or shipper disputes the load?
  3. Can the invoice still be charged back for paperwork issues, claims, or deductions?

If the answers are "bankruptcy only," "you own disputes," and "yes, we can charge it back," then you've primarily purchased accelerated cash flow, not comprehensive credit protection.

For many trucking companies, the real comparison isn't non-recourse factoring versus trade credit insurance . It's expensive cash with limited protection versus comprehensive credit protection paired with lower-cost financing.

If you're currently using a factor, I'd be happy to help you review the agreement and identify exactly which risks are and are not being transferred.

Michael Havemeyer, TRS, TCS
Michael.Havemeyer@highstreetins.com | 484-960-9231

item.content:encoded:
September 28, 2026 Lancaster County will vote Wednesday on an invitation-for-bids for enabling work on the new county prison as PennDOT’s first York I-83 widening section and two Lancaster US-30/PA-72 jobs go to let Oct. 1 and FMCSA English-proficiency comments close Oct. 9.

Watch items (next 10 days)

  • Sept. 30, 9:15 a.m. — Lancaster County Commissioners, Room 701, 150 N. Queen St. Agenda includes an enabling-project IFB for the Lancaster County Correctional Facility, a new court lease at 1351 Elm Avenue, Lobar and Safe Slide construction agreements, countywide electricity purchase authority, and a Community Action Partnership amendment. Matters for prison timing and county contract spend.
  • Sept. 30, 1:30 p.m. — Dauphin County Prison Board of Inspectors at Dauphin County Prison, 501 Mall Road. Regular prison-board business with countywide public-safety implications.
  • Oct. 1, 9:30 a.m. — Lebanon County Commissioners, Room 207, 400 S. 8th St. Follow-up window after the Sept. 17 2–1 vote to advertise a rewritten hotel-tax grant ordinance.
  • Oct. 1 — PennDOT bid openings: York I-83 first-phase widening/Codorus structures; Lancaster US-30/PA-462 interchange improvements (est. $20–25 million) and PA-72 over Chiques Creek bridge rehab ($2.5–5 million). Direct freight-corridor impact.
  • Oct. 7, 10 a.m. — York County Commissioners regular meeting, 28 E. Market St. First scheduled board date after Sept. 23.
  • Oct. 9 — Comment deadline on FMCSA NPRM (91 FR 51422) to codify English-language proficiency as an out-of-service violation. Also Lebanon’s proclaimed Ageism Awareness Day.
  • Early October — Harrisburg Business Administrator Antonio Megna told the ICA Sept. 24 the city aims to put a 2027 budget draft before Mayor Wanda Williams in early October and City Council by Nov. 10; LERTA rewrite targeted for Council in November or December.

Lancaster County

Government

Commissioners D’Agostino (chair), Parsons, and Yoder meet Sept. 30. The live item is the prison enabling IFB after Lancaster Township supervisors approved the land-development plan Sept. 15, clearing the path to building permits. Design was closed in June; consultants have put construction near $469–$500 million and total debt service above $1 billion over 32 years. The Prison Board on Sept. 17 said it will consider an October resolution limiting public comment; Chair Parsons and Controller Scott Wiglesworth said ICE-partnership questions are outside the board’s remit. 2026 millage is already 3.201 (10% over 2025).

Politics / elections

Nov. 3 general: PA-11 Smucker (R) vs. Nancy Mannion (D). SD-36: Sen. James Malone (D) vs. Rep. Tom Jones (R). A Spotlight PA recap of an early-September State Navigate poll had Jones 48–45 in a Trump +15 district.

Business & development

DEP opened a comment period (due Oct. 26) on an air-quality plan approval for Greenfield Road Owner, LLC Phase 2 at 216 Greenfield Road (former LSC/R.R. Donnelley plant): 84 additional diesel generators on top of 72 already approved in Phase 1 (156 total). West Cocalico will close Swamp Bridge Road as soon as Sept. 28 for a $399,978 culvert job (Construction Masters Services), finish targeted Oct. 30.

Other local signal

Lancaster City Council Sept. 30 considers final passage of a capital-budget ordinance. Manheim Township Sept. 28 agenda included a King/Oregon Ag settlement and a county MOU on commodity-flow data.

Lebanon County

Government

Sept. 17 meeting: CYS Administrator Erin Moyer reported FY2025–26 spending of $17.55 million against a $16.06 million certified budget (overrun $1.49 million); county share rose $820,071 to $4.65 million. FY2026–27 county share is projected at $4.15 million (+9%). Juvenile Probation overspent by $1.39 million. Commissioners also hired Vision Government Solutions for Clean and Green work at $4,800 and approved $37,697 in MH/ID/EI contract amendments. Cash on hand after the meeting: $1.84 million.

Politics / elections

SD-48: Sen. Chris Gebhard (R) is the nominee; no Democrat filed in the primary (Wayne Moyer ran a write-in). Hotel-tax rewrite is the near-term local fight: Kuhn/Phillips 2–1 over Litz on Sept. 17 to advertise an ordinance shifting the county’s ~10% / ~$138,000 slice of a $1.38 million program to Visit Lebanon Valley and the Expo Center.

Business & development

North Londonderry supervisors Sept. 21 gave final approval to a second county Chick-fil-A. Palmyra school board Sept. 17 directed administration to advance high-school renovations and additions. The $1.7 billion Inch & Co. South Annville data-center concept (five buildings, ~100 acres off PA-422) remains unfiled.

Other local signal

Lebanon School District scheduled three October public meetings on whether to leave LCCTC; the superintendent said a 50/50 funding model would raise the city’s share about $467,036 a year for 30 years.

York County

Government

Commissioners Wheeler, Burford, and Hoke met Sept. 2 and Sept. 23; next regular date is Oct. 7. Calendar-year 2026 millage is already 7.55 (from 6.90; +9.4%, +$88.40 on a $136,000 average assessment). No new millage action in the last seven days.

Politics / elections

PA-10 (northern York plus Dauphin/Cumberland) is the competitive federal race; PA-11 covers southern York with Lancaster.

Business & development

Quiet in the last seven days on plant expansions, bankruptcies, or industrial-park filings. I-83 first-phase contractor bidding is the freight-facing development item (see PennDOT).

Other local signal

County board calendar is otherwise routine through Oct. 7.

Dauphin County

Government

No new commissioners legislative packet surfaced for the last seven days. Prison Board meets Sept. 30. 2026 county budget already adopted with a 9.75% tax increase (Douglas and Hartwick yes; Pries no).

Politics / elections

F&M College Poll of PA-10 registered voters, Sept. 9–20 (n>350, MoE ±5.7): Janelle Stelson (D) 52%, Rep. Scott Perry (R) 48%. Stelson lost by 1.2 points in 2024; Trump carried the district by 5.2.

Business & development

Harrisburg ICA on Sept. 24 reviewed a rewritten LERTA draft with Business Administrator Antonio Megna and Economic Development Director Edquina Washington. Program has been paused in 2026; city wants Council action in November or December and is hiring a business-development director and LERTA administrator. HCI DP Land Acquisition’s South Hanover quarry data-center filings (two buildings, 401,800 and 195,000 sq ft) remain the outstanding township land-use fight; no new vote this week.

Other local signal

City 2027 budget draft is due to the mayor in early October.

PennDOT & roads

  • US-30, Lancaster (Manheim/East Lampeter): left-lane restrictions 9 a.m.–2 p.m. Sept. 23–25 for inspections on the PA-23, Greenfield Road, and PA-340 bridges over Lincoln Highway.
  • York I-83 widening, first section (south of US-30 to south of Eberts Lane; Codorus/rail/Loucks Mill structure replacement): bids scheduled to open Oct. 1; construction start early 2027. Later sections: US-30/N. George Street interchanges 2029–33; Market Street 2030–34.
  • I-83 South Bridge (Dauphin/Cumberland), MPMS 113754: advertised July 24; let Oct. 29; construction early 2027; ECMS range $1.2–$1.3 billion. Vegetation/early-action work slated to start in October. East Shore Section 3 already under construction toward an October 2027 first-contract finish.
  • US-30/PA-462 interchange, East Lampeter, and PA-72 over Chiques Creek: District 8-0 lettings Oct. 1.
  • I-81 near Carlisle (Cumberland, I-81 freight feed into Dauphin): overnight ramp closures/detours 9 p.m.–6 a.m. in mid-September on the $11.87 million New Enterprise resurfacing job (through August 2027).
  • I-83 Newberry Twp. overlay ($4.68 million, Pennsy Supply) had a Sept. 17 completion target.
  • Statewide: Shapiro administration on Sept. 26 directed $250 million to accelerate 79 paving projects (400+ miles, 44 counties) from the 2026–27 Motor License Fund boost. rabbit transit’s Harrisburg Cameron Street Phase III bid letting had been targeted for September 2026; Phase II vertical construction is underway.

FMCSA / trucking & freight risk

FMCSA’s Aug. 10 NPRM (Docket FMCSA-2026-0826; 91 FR 51422) would write into 49 CFR 391.11(b)(2) that failing English-language proficiency is an out-of-service violation, matching current CVSA criteria and narrowing the Mexico-border-zone exception. Comments close Oct. 9. Agency materials estimate on the order of 9,000 OOS actions a year if finalized. Separately, the Feb. 13 final rule on non-domiciled CDLs (effective March 16) already limits foreign-domiciled CLP/CDL issuance to specified employment-based nonimmigrant statuses. No new PA MCSAP blitz was announced in the last seven days. Credit/ops hook: an OOS ELP finding parks the driver and the load; brokers and shippers running I-81/I-83/US-30 should assume more delayed pickups and tighter driver-pool risk on carriers that staff with limited-English drivers. Non-domiciled CDL tightening is a capacity and receivables issue for any local carrier that hired on those credentials.

Cross-county / Harrisburg items that hit the region

  • Nov. 3 general election: PA-10 (Perry/Stelson) is the Tossup/Lean-D federal race covering Dauphin and northern York; PA-11 (Smucker/Mannion) covers Lancaster and southern York; SD-36 (Malone/Jones) is the targeted Lancaster Senate seat.
  • Data-center air and land-use dockets now sit in Lancaster city (Greenfield Road generators), South Hanover (quarry site), and unfiled in South Annville.
  • I-83 South Bridge let and York I-83 first-phase let will stack construction traffic on the same north–south freight spine into 2027.

1. Diesel jumped about 10 cents while spot rates rose about 2 cents

Source: FreightWaves (Sep 28)

Why it matters: Fuel is outrunning rates, so cash and margins get squeezed first, especially on empty miles

where surcharges don't help. Tender rejections are still about 14%, so carriers keep some rate leverage, but

fuel is the pressure point.

https://www.freightwaves.com/news/diesel-up-10-cents-spot-rates-up-2-margin-squeeze

2. Nebraska eases dyed-diesel and harvest weight rules; governor asks for a 90-day diesel

export pause

Source: Overdrive (Sep 28)

Why it matters: State relief eases harvest cash and operating friction: untaxed dyed diesel use and refunds,

and up to 25% over weight without permits for 90 days. An export pause, if it happens, would be a macro

lever on diesel inventories and pump prices.

https://www.overdriveonline.com/regulations/article/15836000/will-trump-pause-diesel-exports-ag-fuel-haulers-new-regs-relief

3. Montana extends the federal fuel-hauler hours-of-service waiver to in-state gasoline and

diesel moves

Source: Montana Governor's Office (Sep 25)

Why it matters: Executive Order 10-2026 aligns intrastate fuel haulers with the federal waiver through Dec

16, 2026, so in-state fuel supply isn't stuck under tighter state rules. Other cargo is unchanged.

https://news.mt.gov/Governors-Office/Governor-Gianforte-Issues-Executive-Order-to-Extend-Federal-Fuel-Hauling-Flexibility-to-

Montana-Carriers

4. TEN adds 3,000 trailers, taking its fleet to about 85,000, ahead of peak season

Source: Trucking Dive (Sep 25)

Why it matters: Trailer access is becoming a working-capital and load-acceptance constraint. Leasing

capacity with newer telematics can decide whether a carrier takes freight or passes.

https://www.truckingdive.com/news/leasing-provider-adds-3k-trailers-anticipating-greater-demand/831050/

5. FMCSA seeks comment on nine hearing-exemption applications for CMV drivers

Source: Federal Register (Sep 28; comments due Oct 28)

Why it matters: A routine medical-exemption docket, but another small channel for driver supply and

qualification while non-domiciled CDL and training-school crackdowns tighten entry elsewhere.

https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/28/2026-19808/qualification-of-drivers-exemption-applications-hearing

item.title: Freight Intel Brief — September 25, 2026 PennDOT opened the first $250 million wave of statewide Rapid Deployment paving
item.content:encoded:
I-83 South Bridge heads to an Oct. 29 let, while Lancaster’s prison PREA counseling remains unresolved and Lebanon locked in higher Children & Youth costs.

Watch items (next 10 days)

• Thu Oct 1, 9:30 a.m. — Lebanon County Commissioners regular meeting (first Thursday). Follow-on hotel-tax ordinance draft (2–1 on Sept. 17) and CYS cost pressure. Why it matters: millage and tourism-tax administration.

• Mon Sept 29, 2 p.m. — North Lebanon Township budget workshop (more sessions Oct. 6+). Why it matters: local paving, fire, and land-development cash.

• Mon Oct 5 — Penn Manor School Board (after Committee of the Whole). Why it matters: school tax timing against Lancaster’s 2027 reassessment.

• October (date TBA) — Lancaster County Prison Board resolution on public-comment limits. Why it matters: board time vs. ICE/PREA contract debate while a ~$469–500 million prison bid package is prepared.

• Through Oct. 5 — Confirm District 8 night/weekend restrictions on I-81, I-83, US-30, US-222, PA-283 via 511PA; I-83 South Bridge bid clock runs to Oct. 29. Why it matters: Harrisburg–York–Lancaster truck routing.

Lancaster County

Government

Commissioners met Sept. 23 (agenda amended Sept. 22); item-level votes were not posted in open news accounts this week. Prison PREA sexual-assault counseling has been dark since 2023; YWCA Lancaster and county counsel are still negotiating after billing and security-protocol disputes. Commissioner Alice Yoder pressed the issue at a work session; Chair Josh Parsons and Ray D’Agostino said staff—not the board—should pick vendors. Prior rate was $25/hour; YWCA has offered no-charge service since 2024. Prison Board will take up public-comment limits next month after ICE-agreement testimony crowded meetings. New-prison design phase is closed; next step is construction bid packages on a former Lancaster Township farm site (~$469 million hard cost cited earlier; consultants have also used ~$500 million).

Politics / elections

A countywide library-tax referendum is on the Nov. 3 ballot: “Shall the County of Lancaster establish a dedicated Library tax … at the rate of .55 mills…?” Petition was accepted Sept. 4; local TV confirmed ballot status mid-September. Unadjusted, .55 mills was estimated near $44 million under preliminary 2027 assessments; a revenue-neutral reset could cut the rate toward ~.31 mills / ~$25 million. SD-36 (northern Lancaster): incumbent Sen. James Malone (D) vs. Rep. Tom Jones (R); a Sept. 11–13 State Navigate likely-voter poll (n=915, ±3.2) had Jones 48–45 with leaners, 7% undecided. PA-11 (Smucker) had no new local official action this week.

Business & development

Quiet this week. Farmland preservation and the 2027 reassessment remain the structural tax story (notices dated June 15; county millage reset due December).

Other local signal

School boards (Penn Manor Oct. 5; CTC JOC met Sept. 24) are the near-term public-service venues.

Lebanon County

Government

Sept. 17 commissioners meeting: FY 2025–26 Children & Youth spent $17.55 million vs. $16.06 million certified (county share $4.65 million, +$820,071). FY 2026–27 CYS implementation budget $20.73 million approved; FY 2027–28 needs-based $20.02 million. Administrator Jamie Wolgemuth called the figures “huge”; Commissioner Bob Phillips said he was “dumbfounded.” Hotel-tax grant ordinance first draft passed 2–1 (Jo Ellen Litz no). Assessment board cut two commercial assessments (Walmart Lehman St. $7.96M→$5.21M; North Londonderry $6.98M→$4.50M). Nov. 3 ballot approved; 94,283 registered voters.

Politics / elections

No new candidate filings this week. SD-48 (Gebhard) is not on the 2026 ballot cycle highlighted in local coverage this week.

Business & development

North Londonderry approved a second county Chick-fil-A (Sept. 21). North Lebanon unanimously approved a six-building self-storage project on a ~6-acre industrial site on Suzy Street and granted time extensions on R&L Carriers and LCW Holdings land-development plans. CFA Local Share Account gaming grants: nearly $2 million countywide, including Union Twp. $697,870 for Northern Lebanon Fire & EMS vehicles and North Cornwall $200,000 highway-garage expansion. Corn/soy yields called average to slightly below average.

Other local signal

School capital: Cornwall-Lebanon paid $3.8 million in Cedar Crest renovation bills; Annville-Cleona is still debating a $102.5 million renovation estimate; Palmyra advanced high-school additions; Lebanon SD is soliciting taxpayer input on possible LCCTC withdrawal.

York County

Government

Commissioners’ week was operationally quiet in published coverage. Justice & Public Safety Committee met Sept. 23 on 911 evaluation and an EMS strategic plan.

Politics / elections

No new countywide ballot-question or row-office official action in the last seven days.

Business & development

BAE Systems Automation Training Center and Weldon Solutions Robotics Lab opened (Manufacturers’ Association of Central PA; TIDE/DoW OLDCC and DCED funds). Defense manufacturers in the midstate report ~400 current openings. Separate from SC York mix-ups in some aggregators: PA York industrial pipeline remains active (Expressway Commerce Center 674,000 sf underway; York County Trade Center ~376,000 sf marketed). Multiple proposed data-center sites are tracked in Peach Bottom, Conewago, West Manchester, Fairview, East Manchester, and Windsor townships; none had a new county vote this week.

Other local signal

Quiet on schools/taxes this week.

Dauphin County

Government

Commissioners held a 2027 budget hearing Sept. 22 and a regular meeting Sept. 23 (video posted; item-level dollars not summarized in open text). No millage vote this week.

Politics / elections

PA-10 (Perry) had no new local official development this week. Harrisburg city: no new millage action in the last seven days.

Business & development

Quiet aside from I-83 South Bridge procurement (see PennDOT). A nonprofit purchased a $670,000 Harrisburg lot to relocate an encampment off PennDOT-owned land ahead of bridge work.

Other local signal

Transit (CAT) and county human-services dollars were not in new published votes this week.

PennDOT & roads

I-83 South Bridge (Dauphin/Cumberland, SR 0083-094 / ECMS 113754): advertised July 24; mandatory pre-bid was Aug. 19; let Oct. 29; construction start cited as January 2027. Cost $1.1–$1.3 billion; $500 million federal grant. Superloads already banned; use I-81 or Turnpike. Two lanes each way planned for most of the job. Related East Shore I-83 packages: $154.7 million and $132.7 million (19th–29th St., Cameron St. interchange). US-322 / Grayson–Chambers Hill (Swatara): $38.6 million. Maclay Street bridge over NS (Harrisburg): $41.1 million.

York : I-83 widening Route 30 to east of Eberts Lane / Mill Creek relocation ~$200 million (2026–2029). I-83 Newberry resurfacing $4.7 million had a Sept. 17 completion target. US-30 Hellam resurfacing/bridge preservation $17.2 million.

Lancaster : US-222 / US-30 interchange and 222 widening, Manheim Twp., $72.2 million; US-30/462 East Lampeter $22 million; US-30 Salisbury/Sadsbury resurfacing $4.4 million.

Lebanon : PA-72 Quentin Rd. $7 million; PA-72 Ebenezer Rd. $3.5 million.

Statewide hook with local trucking impact: Sept. 24 PennDOT/Shapiro announcement — first $250 million of $775 million Motor License Fund Rapid Deployment paving (79 projects, 400+ miles, 44 counties). Check District 8 list for four-county segments. I-81 Carlisle overnight paving is Cumberland but feeds Dauphin/Lebanon freight. Use 511PA for lane closures.

FMCSA / trucking & freight risk

No new FMCSA newsroom release dated Sept. 18–25. Still in force: English Language Proficiency is an out-of-service item at roadside (policy MC-SEE-2026-0002, Apr. 16); HOS Flexible Sleeper Berth and Split Duty Period pilots advanced Aug. 27; ELD operator’s-manual-in-cab rule rescinded effective July 22; multiple ELD models remain on the revoked list (using one = no ELD). Aug. 31 interagency trucking-fraud initiative is the latest enforcement posture.

Credit/ops line : ELP OOS and revoked-ELD OOS can idle trucks and interrupt receivables; confirm carriers on four-county lanes are on a current registered ELD and can pass an English inquiry.

Cross-county / Harrisburg items that hit the region

Nov. 3 general election is the binding local date: Lancaster library millage, SD-36 Malone/Jones, PA-10 and PA-11, plus county row offices. I-83 South Bridge let (Oct. 29) is the region’s largest freight-network event. Gaming LSA grants and hotel-tax administration (Lebanon) are the live tourism-tax files. Data-center siting is a campaign issue in SD-36 and a permitting issue in York townships; no four-county moratorium vote this week.

• https://lebtown.com/2026/09/21/lebanon-county-children-youth-services-sees-huge-costs-in-2025-26/

• https://lebtown.com/2026/09/18/lebanon-county-projects-land-nearly-2-million-in-gaming-funded-state-grants/

• https://lebtown.com/2026/09/23/n-lebanon-supes-approve-suzy-street-self-storage-narrows-dr-townhouse-subdivisions/

• https://www.abc27.com/local-business/automation-training-center-and-robotics-lab-opens-in-york-county/

• https://www.pa.gov/agencies/penndot/projects-near-you/district-8-projects/i-83-south-bridge-project

• https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/newsroom/press-releases

item.title: The Consumer Is Not Collapsing. That Is the Most Expensive Half-Truth in Freight.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The consumer is not collapsing. That sentence is true, and it is the most expensive half-truth in freight right now. Households are still spending — more selectively, more on essentials, and in one case out of five, past the paycheck.

This week those household trade-offs showed up where they always do for this industry: on the bankruptcy docket, on the import print, and in the aging reports of companies that sell on terms. If you haul freight, broker it, finance it, or insure the receivable behind it, this is not a retail-color story. It is a working-capital story.

🛒 The household is still standing. The budget is not.

EY-Parthenon’s Wave 6 U.S. Consumer Sentiment Survey, fielded the last week of June, is the cleanest recent read on why freight demand feels “fine” until it isn’t.

•  Sentiment is soft but stable month over month. Shoppers are cautious, not panicked — and they are still buying discretionary goods, just with a sharper pencil.

•  Roughly one in five households spent more than they earned last month. More than half saved nothing. Among households that dipped into savings or debt, concern about groceries, healthcare, transportation, and housing ran nearly twice as high as among households that covered expenses with income.

•  That 20 percent figure is not confined to low earners. About a quarter of high-income households in the sample also failed to cover the month with income. Confidence and cash flow are not the same variable.

•  More than 60 percent of respondents have said they expect a U.S. recession within three years — and they have said it for a year running. Soft prints and a hard-landing thesis can live in the same survey.

Why it matters for trucking and credit. When households stretch, retailers stretch. When retailers stretch, distributors wait, carriers wait, and someone in that chain is now your past due. Accounts receivable are often 40 percent or more of an SME’s assets. Every load moved on terms is a loan. “The consumer is resilient” is a sentiment. Capacity to pay is a cash-flow statement.

The weather under the print. Prices and household real balances are not only a story about last month’s CPI print. They are the market’s running judgment of whether future taxes, tariffs, and spending restraint will actually back the public-debt path. Tariffs are a fiscal tool, not just a trade tool. They reprice imported goods, pull purchasing power out of the household, and leave the private sector to absorb the adjustment — first at the grocery aisle, then on the payable. The headline is the spark. Cash is the dry grass.

⛽ Essentials crowded out the load board.

Wave 6 is specific about where the money is going, and where it is leaving.

•  Inflation, tariffs, domestic politics, and geopolitical conflict remain the heaviest household stressors, with no real relief versus a year ago. Groceries sit at the top of the “greatly concerned” list.

•  Transportation anxiety cooled from the April spike after crude eased when the late-June U.S.–Iran memorandum reopened the Strait of Hormuz. Most respondents now expect gasoline back under $3.50 within a year. Housing affordability and weak wage growth did not get that relief.

•  To offset higher gas prices, 32 percent of households re-evaluated leisure and entertainment budgets; 27 percent re-evaluated food. Net spend is still rising in groceries, transportation, housing, and pet care. It is being pulled from restaurants, travel, apparel, entertainment, home improvement, and fitness.

•  A majority say they can still cut dining out, beauty and personal care, and apparel without making daily life “meaningfully worse.” EY-Parthenon flags dining, travel, apparel, and entertainment as the categories most exposed to the next demand shock.

Why it matters for trucking and credit. Those “room to cut” categories are less-than-truckload (LTL), parcel, and import-container categories. Grocery and basic transportation freight have a different risk profile than restaurant supply, apparel importers, leisure goods, and home décor. Traditional commercial towers cover the truck, the cargo, the driver, and the lawsuit. They do not cover the unpaid invoice from the shipper whose end market just got cut. Underwrite the end market, not just the bill-to name.

🚛 Sixteen carriers in four weeks is not a vibe. It is a docket.

FreightWaves reported this week that at least 16 trucking, delivery, and transportation companies entered bankruptcy between late August and September 21. The list is not one niche, one region, or one fleet size.

•  Xoco Transport (Hidalgo, Texas): 40-plus tractors, about 70 trailers, Chapter 11, September 16.

•  Globemaster Inc. (Bolingbrook, Illinois): 51 power units, assets $500K–$1M against $1M–$10M of liabilities, Chapter 11, September 15.

•  CLJ Transporting (Auburndale, Florida), an Amazon Delivery Service Partner: 18 trucks, 30 drivers, Chapter 11, September 15.

•  Around them: Jett Transport & Materials, Mill Creek Logistics-Illinois, RP Hay Hauling, Truckload LLC / Expedite Express, Pacer Transport, and a string of one- to six-truck Chapter 7 liquidations in Illinois, Texas, and California.

Chapter 11 is not a shutdown. Some of these fleets will reorganize and keep rolling. Every filing is still a credit event — fuel, tires, leases, warehouse charges, factoring, broker settlements, cargo in transit, and the shipper waiting on a receivable.

Why it matters for trucking and credit. The September docket was not national accounts. It was the 1- to 50-truck layer, plus a last-mile contractor sitting inside a giant’s network. If you sell parts, fuel, insurance, or freight to that layer, concentration and uninsured accounts receivable are the issue — not “the market feels better than 2023.” A company can be fully insured on the traditional towers and still fail on a single unpaid receivable.

Who absorbs the adjustment. Volume holes and cost spikes do not land evenly. Large, well-positioned networks reroute, renegotiate, and wait out the court. Thinly capitalized operators — the ones without a political or financial sponsor — absorb the adjustment in cash. That is not a morality play. It is how a shakeout looks when connected capital has more options than a five-truck fleet in Midland. The people with the least slack absorb the most of the shift.

📦 Imports fell 4.5 percent. That is a lane story and a new-buyer story.

Descartes Datamyne, as reported by FreightWaves on September 23, found U.S. imports down 4.5 percent in the twelve months after Liberation Day tariffs (May 2025–April 2026 versus the prior year). Maritime import volumes fell 4.3 percent.

•  China-origin volumes dropped sharply. Mexico gained share as the top U.S. source. Vietnam and Taiwan picked up redirected flow.

•  The trade deficit narrowed because inbound cargo slowed — not because outbound cargo boomed.

•  After the Supreme Court canceled the IEEPA tariffs, imports were up 9 percent year over year in April 2026. Trade policy is still a volume switch. It is not a reason to assume the next twelve months refill every trailer that sat empty in 2025.

Why it matters for trucking and credit. Mexico-up, China-down is a customs story and a drayage story. It is also a new-counterparty story. Redirected supply chains create new legal entities, shorter operating histories, and more intermediated credit. Treat the new supplier — and the U.S. buyer standing behind a familiar brand — as a new file. The unprotected asset is not the container. It is the invoice attached to a name you have not underwritten yet.

Incidence is not written in the statute. Tariff architecture is written in Washington and litigated in court. The incidence is paid on the dock and on the payable. Who captures the reroute, who eats the empty mile, and who gets a hearing when the rule changes are not decided by the owner-operator with 39 trucks and a fuel card. Policy shocks show up in freight as delayed orders and stretched payables before they show up as headlines about “the supply chain.”

🚄 Brightline is the large-cap rhyme.

Florida’s Brightline is preparing an imminent Chapter 11 filing in New Jersey to restructure roughly $5.5 billion in debt, according to people familiar with the matter cited by The Wall Street Journal this week.

•  The plan, as reported: keep the operating trains outside the filing so service continues; put the holding company in court; cut the debt load toward $2.7 billion.

•  Ridership never grew fast enough to service a capital structure built on municipal bonds and private-equity sponsorship. Leverage met a demand curve that did not arrive on schedule.

•  Different mode than a 40-tractor fleet in Hidalgo. Same pattern: a demand shortfall meeting a balance sheet that assumed the volume would show up.

Why it matters for trucking and credit. Sixteen small carriers will not lead the evening news next to a $5.5 billion passenger railroad. They will lead a lot of aging reports. Watch which names get a reorganization path that protects operations, and which names get a Chapter 7 and a sold-off trailer. That split is the credit lesson, not the headline. Downstream suppliers still holding open invoices do not get a seat at the restructuring table unless the receivable was protected before the filing.

Final thought

Consumers are not collapsing. That is why retail sales prints keep surprising people who only read the recession question. The less comfortable news is how that stability is being purchased: fewer dinners out, thinner apparel tickets, savings drawn down, cards carried a month longer, and a fifth of households already spending past the paycheck.

Freight is where that behavior becomes a missed settlement. Resilience is a sentiment. Capacity to pay is a cash-flow statement. Traditional coverage does not close that gap. Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) turns the receivable from an unsecured promise into a protected asset. Supply Chain Finance (SCF) turns time into cash against that protected receivable. Together they are not a product pitch. They are the missing half of 360-degree risk management — protection plus velocity — so an SME can keep selling through a mix like this without betting the company.

TCI answers “what if they don’t pay?” · SCF answers “what if they pay too slowly?” · Together they answer “how do we keep selling through this?”

If you sell on terms into this demand mix, the work this quarter is unglamorous and specific: re-segment the book by end market, watch days-to-pay before the account goes past due, stress the 1- to 50-truck layer and anyone who vends to it, and put a number on the uninsured receivable. “They’ve always paid in 35 days” is not analysis when the household on the other end of the chain is already in the hole.

Let’s talk

I send The Risk and Resilience Report to agents and transportation clients who want 2026 receivables underwritten category by category, buyer by buyer — not on the sentence “the consumer is fine.” If this week’s mix is already in your aging report, pick up the phone. The first meeting should produce a map of the receivable book and a decision about which names are the business and which names are the bet. Not a bind. A conversation.

item.title: Four-County + Freight Intel Brief — September 21, 2026, Lancaster’s Nov. 3
item.content:encoded:
library-tax fight and a county congestion-study contract landed in the same week Smucker backed a federal data-center ratepayer bill and PennDOT kept overnight closures on I-81 and Routes 72/322.

Watch items (next 10 days)

  • Sept. 22 — Lancaster MPO meets (packet posted Sept. 16). Congestion-study follow-through and TIP priorities affect US-30/222/462 freight routing.
  • Sept. 22 — Lancaster City Council, 6:30 p.m.; Conestoga Valley and Hempfield school boards. City and school millage sit on top of the 2027 reassessment.
  • Sept. 22 — South Lebanon Township supervisors, 7 p.m. Boundary ordinance with North Cornwall still pending.
  • Sept. 23 — Lancaster County commissioners, 9:15 a.m., Government Center. First regular session after the Sept. 16 evening meeting in Christiana.
  • Sept. 23 — York County commissioners. Agenda posted; no major tax item flagged in public coverage.
  • Sept. 20–24, 9 p.m.–6 a.m. — I-81 ramp closures continue near Carlisle (MM 47–52). Last night of this cycle is Sept. 24.
  • Oct. 1 — Lebanon County commissioners’ next regular meeting (first/third Thursdays). Hotel-tax ordinance follow-up if not closed Sept. 17.
  • Oct. 9 (just beyond 10 days) — FMCSA English-language proficiency OOS NPRM comments close. Plan comments now.

Lancaster County

Government

Commissioners were scheduled Sept. 16 to award a $35,685 Michael Baker International contract for an MPO congestion-management study due Jan. 1, 2027 (top 25 bottlenecks and ramps). Commissioner Ray D’Agostino chairs the MPO. Evening session was at Christiana Borough; next regular meeting is Sept. 23.

Reassessment appeals are lighter than 2018 (~2% of 189,358 taxable parcels). Countywide values are up about 77% on current office figures (earlier preliminary maps showed ~90%). New values take effect Jan. 1, 2027, for municipalities; school millage uses them in 2027–28. Hearings were expected to finish by mid-October.

PDE began a financial audit of the School District of Lancaster on Aug. 17; the board confirmed it Sept. 14 after a projected $27.8 million 2026–27 deficit and summer borrowing. On Sept. 16 CFO Marcia Stokes said the district repaid a $10 million First National Bank loan and about $19 million borrowed from capital reserve; general fund was $24 million as of Sept. 1.

Politics / elections

Nov. 3 ballot question: 0.55-mill dedicated library tax (~$55 per $100,000 of assessed value; ~$44 million in 2027 on June reassessment data; millage may be cut to stay revenue-neutral). SD-36 rivals Sen. James Malone (D) and Rep. Tom Jones (R-98) both said they will vote no.

Rep. Lloyd Smucker (PA-11) voted with a 417–3 House majority for the Ratepayer Protection Act, requiring state utility commissions to make large data centers pay for added generation rather than shift costs to ratepayers.

Business & development

York Water Co. agreed to buy Paradise Township Sewer Authority assets (Lancaster County), adding 700+ wastewater customers, pending PUC approval.

Retail/hospitality: Grotto Pizza opening in Manheim Twp.; AutoZone stores in Willow Street and East Lampeter; Savers Lancaster Twp. set to open Oct. 1; Cartel Brewing taking Fetish’s Rock Lititz space.

Another local signal

Lancaster Capital Day downtown festival is Sept. 26. Ephrata Fair runs Sept. 22–26; West Lampeter Fair Sept. 23–25.

Lebanon County

Government

Commissioners on Sept. 3 voted 2–1 (Jo Ellen Litz no) to advertise an ordinance shifting the county’s 10% hotel-tax slice (~$138,000 of a projected $1.38 million 2026 pool) to Lebanon Valley Expo Center (70%) and Visit Lebanon Valley (30%). If adopted, county grant administration would end Dec. 31. Item was teed for Sept. 17; no published vote found as of this brief. Next regular meeting: Oct. 1.

South Lebanon supervisors approved a boundary-correction agreement with North Cornwall (about seven properties; ordinance expected in October). Pension MMOs set: police $288,807; non-uniform DB $223,576; DC $45,924. Next meeting Sept. 22.

Politics / elections

No new countywide ballot action this week. Midterm mail-in calendar is unchanged locally (register by Oct. 19; request mail ballots by Oct. 27).

Business & development

North Annville supervisors enacted a data-center ordinance Sept. 14. Union Township already has a restrictive data-center ordinance (No. 197). West Lebanon’s draft data-center ordinance is at county review (30-day clock) with a water-capacity question on the record.

Palmyra Borough waived land-development timing for Irvin Services’ 24,000-sf painting shop at the former Cadillac Motel (977 E. Main), about 12 added jobs. Millcreek approved a 10,080-sf Fox Masonry shop on S. Sheridan Road.

Lebanon Valley Chamber Foundation micro-grants (up to $3,000; $30,000 pool) are open Sept. 14–Oct. 23 for firms/nonprofits with ≤25 employees.

Another local signal

Jackson Township advertised a millage hike from 0.18 to 0.30 and a $52 local services tax (split vote on the millage ad). American House Personal Care Home slated to close mid-November.

York County

Government

Commissioners met Sept. 16 (27-minute session). No published tax, millage, or contract headline from that meeting. Next session Sept. 23. The Aug. 26 tornado disaster declaration ran through Sept. 20. 2026 county millage is already set at 7.55 (0.65-mill / 9.4% hike adopted Dec. 2025 on a $283.7 million general fund).

Politics / elections

County elections office said mail-in procedures are unchanged after the summer high-court ruling on the federal mail-ballot order. Deadlines: register Oct. 19; request mail ballot Oct. 27; received by 8 p.m. Nov. 3.

Business & development

York Water’s Paradise Twp. (Lancaster) wastewater deal is the week’s main utility transaction touching the county’s operator. Chanceford Crossing wastewater was acquired earlier in 2026.

Other local signal

Quiet on county industrial-park or warehouse announcements this week.

Dauphin County

Government

Commissioners met Sept. 16; no new millage or budget action in public coverage. 2026 budget already includes a 9.75% property-tax increase (Douglas and Hartwick yes; Pries no). Prison Board’s May resolution still requires a judicial warrant—not a civil ICE detainer—to hold or transfer inmates.

Politics / elections

PA-10 (Rep. Scott Perry) remains the federal race overlaying Dauphin and northern York; no new county row-office filing item this week.

Business & development

Veolia boil-water advisory remained in effect Sept. 14 in parts of Susquehanna and Lower Paxton townships after a Linglestown Road main break (Laurelwood / Fargreen / portions of Continental, Melbourne, Forest Hills, Linglestown).

State Museum of Pennsylvania programs shifted to Dauphin County Library System’s Love Memorial Library during a $79.3 million renovation through early 2029. First session was Sept. 16.

Other local signal

No new farmland-preservation or transit-capital vote reported this week.

PennDOT & roads

  • I-81, Cumberland (feeds Dauphin/Lebanon freight): Overnight paving and ramp closures Sun–Thu, 9 p.m.–6 a.m., through Sept. 24, MM 47–52 (Exits 48/49/52). Contractor New Enterprise Stone & Lime; contract $11,872,635; completion target Aug. 27, 2027. This week’s posted nights: Exit 52 ramps (Sept. 20–21), Exit 49 to PA-641 (Sept. 22). Check 511PA.
  • I-83, Newberry Twp., York: Overlay/drainage $4,678,000 (Pennsy Supply). PennDOT listed completion Sept. 17, 2026. Confirm live restrictions on 511PA.
  • PA-72 / US-322, Lebanon (North/West Cornwall, Cornwall Borough): $7,009,000 resurfacing (Pennsy Supply) from the Lancaster line to Rocherty Road. Nighttime milling/paving detours resumed after Labor Day (6 p.m.–6 a.m. patterns on 72 and the 322 concurrency). Completion Dec. 3, 2026. Alternate: PA-117 / Pinch / Cider Press and PA-419/501.
  • Lancaster MPO: Congestion study will re-rank US-30/222/462 bottlenecks used for TIP selection. No new SCTA / rabbittransit / CAT capital award found this week.

FMCSA / trucking & freight risk

  • Fuel HOS waiver (issued Sept. 16, 90 days): Drivers hauling gasoline or diesel may operate up to 16 hours in a 24-hour window if the carrier is in good standing (no conditional rating or active OOS). Fatigue rest still required; incidents must be reported to FMCSA within two business days. Why credit/ops cares: peak harvest and heating-season fuel runs get extra legally usable hours; carriers with poor SMS/ratings are excluded.
  • ELP as OOS — NPRM comments due Oct. 9 (Docket FMCSA-2026-0826; 49 CFR 390/391). Proposal would codify English-language proficiency as an out-of-service criterion aligned with CVSA NAS criteria. DOT says 26,000+ unqualified drivers already pulled under current enforcement. Why it matters: a failed roadside ELP check parks the truck and the load; AR/insurance exposure on brokers using non-domiciled or mixed-language fleets.
  • HOS flexible sleeper-berth (6/4, 5/5) and split-duty-period pilots remain open under DOT’s “Pro-Trucker Package.” ELD cab-manual requirement was rescinded effective July 22, 2026. No PA MCSAP blitz notice found for these four counties this week.

Cross-county / Harrisburg items that hit the region

Data-center siting and power-cost allocation is now simultaneous at three levels: House Ratepayer Protection Act (Smucker yes), Lebanon township ordinances (North Annville enacted; Union and West Lebanon already moving), and Lancaster MPO congestion work on the same corridors that would serve warehouse/data loads. Statewide LSA applications opened Sept. 1 and close Nov. 30 (up to $1 million, no match). Nov. 3 midterms: PA-10, PA-11, SD-36, and Lancaster’s library-tax question.

Sources

  • https://lancasteronline.com/news/politics/malone-jones-say-lancaster-county-library-tax-would-hurt-the-36th-district/article_79cc2604-3f3d-416f-b727-bbf8c10e29f8.html
  • https://lancasteronline.com/news/politics/rep-smucker-supports-bill-to-protect-ratepayers-from-high-costs-brought-on-by-data-centers/article_2fe2fffd-bdea-41f8-bf9f-4b9f93129caa.html
  • https://lancasteronline.com/news/local/lancaster-county-to-commission-traffic-congestion-study/article_b9987528-3818-4597-865a-d0a2de82ac1c.html
  • https://lancasteronline.com/news/local/pa-education-department-auditing-school-district-of-lancaster-district-officials-confirm/article_fa29e551-07bb-4dae-8165-afb1e0543d87.html
  • https://lancasteronline.com/news/local/school-district-of-lancaster-board-told-of-improving-financial-position/article_ac2e407b-7b6f-4d32-b62f-49e085264d2b.html
  • https://co.lancaster.pa.us/AgendaCenter/County-Commissioners-Public-Meetings-3
  • https://lancastercountyplanning.org/AgendaCenter
  • https://lebtown.com/2026/09/08/lebanon-county-commissioners-may-exit-hotel-tax-grant-program/
  • https://lebtown.com/2026/09/14/south-lebanon-township-approves-boundary-correction-agreement/
  • https://www.abc27.com/local-news/york-water-company-to-acquire-local-wastewater-system/
  • https://www.abc27.com/news/traffic/paving-will-cause-overnight-ramp-closures-on-i-81-in-cumberland-county/
  • https://www.abc27.com/news/traffic/nighttime-detours-resuming-on-route-72-322-in-lebanon-county/
  • https://www.pa.gov/agencies/penndot/news-and-media/newsroom/district-8/2026/i-83-drainage-project-in-newberry-twp-york-co
  • https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/trumps-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-takes-action-lower-fuel-costs

item.title: What's Happening in the Lower Susquehanna Valley
item.content:encoded:
Watch items (next 10 days)

  • Sept. 18–21 (7 p.m. Fri–6 a.m. Mon): Northbound US-222 right-lane closure at the North Church Street bridge, West Earl Twp. (Brownstown/Rothsville). Freight on 222 should allow extra time.
  • Sept. 20–23, 9 p.m.–6 a.m.: Overnight I-81 ramp paving/closures MM 47–52 near Carlisle (Cumberland), Exits 48–52. Detours use PA-641, PA-34, PA-74, US-11. Hits I-81 through traffic into Dauphin.
  • Through Oct. 19: I-81 southbound Exit 65 (US-11/15 Marysville/Enola) exit ramp closed (511PA). Dauphin/Perry hook.
  • Sept. 23, 10 a.m.: York County Commissioners regular meeting, 28 E. Market St. Next posted legislative date after Sept. 16.
  • Week of Sept. 23: Lancaster Commissioners typically meet Wednesday 9:15 a.m.; Dauphin Commissioners meet Wednesdays 10 a.m. (workshop/legislative rotation). Check posted agendas.
  • October (date TBD): Lancaster County Prison Board to consider a public-comment time-limit resolution.
  • Now–~Oct. 9: FMCSA English-language proficiency / OOS NPRM comment window (docket FMCSA-2026-0826). Operations/HR risk for carriers running I-81/I-83/US-30.

Lancaster County

Government

Lancaster Township supervisors on Sept. 15 approved the land-development plan for the new county prison (about 400,000 sq. ft., 1,046 beds). Engineer Ben Webber said the county can now seek building permits. Design was approved in June; bid solicitation has no public date. Cost is cited at about $500 million; PFM bond options earlier this year put total taxpayer cost above $1 billion over 32 years including interest. Target opening remains 2029, subject to change.

Prison Board Chair Josh Parsons said Sept. 16 the board will consider next month time limits on public comment. Parsons, Commissioner Ray D’Agostino, and Controller Scott Wiglesworth said ICE-partnership comments are outside the board’s remit; Commissioner Alice Yoder backed time limits but not topic limits.

Commissioners this week approved a $208,520 conservation easement on the 52-acre Aaron F. and Naomi S. Stoltzfus farm in Colerain Twp. (sold at 48% of appraisal). County total preserved farmland: 126,123 acres.

Politics / elections

Rep. Lloyd Smucker (PA-11) voted with the 417–3 House majority Sept. 16 for H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act. The bill directs state utility commissions to consider requiring data centers ≥100 MW to pay incremental generation/transmission/distribution costs. It now goes to the Senate.

SD-36 candidates James Malone (D) and Tom Jones (R) both oppose a county library tax. “Vote Yes 4 Libraries” filed 7,282 signatures Sept. 4 for a Nov. 3 referendum at 0.55 mills (~$44 million if unadjusted; ~0.31 mills / ~$25 million if revenue-neutral after reassessment). Challenge window closed Sept. 11; ballot status is with the solicitor.

Business & development

Commissioner Matt Schulte said the proposed 12-month data-center moratorium is off. A task force will study siting, power-rate effects, water use/discharge, and size. County zoning does not currently list data centers; a pending zoning change is paused until the task force reports.

West Donegal supervisors Sept. 14 accepted a petition to rezone the ~87-acre Minnich farm at 4436 Bossler Road from rural to agricultural so it can qualify for a county ag easement.

Federal court Sept. 16: a former federal prosecutor will be appointed counsel for Lancaster businessman Daryl Heller in his $402 million securities-fraud case.

Other local signal

School District of Lancaster CFO Marcia Stokes told the Sept. 15 board the district has repaid intra-year loans and improved its cash position after the $300.8 million 2026–27 budget (4.7% tax hike).

Lebanon County

Government

Commissioners on Sept. 3 voted 2–1 (Jo Ellen Litz opposed) to advertise an ordinance shifting the county’s 10% hotel-tax slice (~$138,000 of a projected $1.38 million 2026 program) to Lebanon Valley Expo Center (70%) and Visit Lebanon Valley (30%). Administrator Jamie Wolgemuth said Sept. 17 was the target vote; if adopted, the county role ends Dec. 31. Confirm minutes.

Politics / elections

Quiet this week beyond midterm/mail-ballot administration already reported in early September (county received ~$472,000 in election-grant funds).

Business & development

West Lebanon Township said Sept. 8 a $125 water-system fee will end December 2026, a year early. Commissioner Jo Ellen Litz, speaking as a resident, asked how a data-center user would be required to buy Authority water if township pumping exceeds 50,000 gpd.

Other local signal

Chair Mike Kuhn recognized Dinosaur Park graffiti-removal volunteers Sept. 11 in South Londonderry Twp. Quiet otherwise.

York County

Government

Commissioners met Sept. 16 (video posted; ~28 minutes). No major millage, contract, or prison action was reported in local coverage this week. Next regular meeting Sept. 23.

Politics / elections

Elections office has said mail-ballot procedures for Nov. 3 are unchanged for now (request deadline Oct. 27; ballots due 8 p.m. Election Day). PA-10 (Perry vs. Stelson) covers northern York and all of Dauphin; PA-11 (Smucker) covers southern York.

Business & development

Quiet in the last seven days on plant expansions, industrial parks, or large real-estate filings in York PA papers.

Other local signal

One-year mark Sept. 17 of the North Codorus Township ambush that killed three Northern York County Regional Police detectives. Public-safety staffing remains a budget driver from the adopted 2026 county budget (7.55 mills after a 0.65-mill / 9.4% hike).

Dauphin County

Government

No new commissioner votes of countywide fiscal weight reported in the last seven days. Board continues Wednesday 10 a.m. meetings. 2026 millage already in effect after the Dec. 2025 9.75% hike (Douglas and Hartwick yes; Pries no).

Politics / elections

PA-10 rematch: Rep. Scott Perry (R) vs. Janelle Stelson (D). District includes all of Dauphin and northern York. Midterms are Nov. 3.

Business & development

Quiet this week on major plant, warehouse, or data-center filings.

Other local signal

Harrisburg city government had no new countywide fiscal action in the last seven days. Prior 2026 mayor–council budget litigation was settled in February.

PennDOT & roads

  • US-222, Lancaster (West Earl): NB right lane closed Fri 7 p.m.–Mon 6 a.m. for bridge work over N. Church St. Part of an $8.49 million, 3.3-mile pavement job (New Enterprise Stone & Lime) from Bushong Rd. to Pool Rd. SB off-ramp deceleration lane was slated to reopen Friday 6 a.m.
  • US-30 / US-222 interchange, Lancaster: Multi-year $72.2 million JD Eckman job; completion target Sept. 3, 2027. No new full-weekend closure announced this week.
  • I-81, Cumberland (feeds Dauphin): Overnight ramp closures Sept. 20–23, MM 47–52 (Exits 48, 49, 52). Patching/paving plus bridge parapet work.
  • I-81, Dauphin: SB Exit 65 (US-11/15 Marysville/Enola) ramp closed through Oct. 19 per 511PA.
  • I-83, Dauphin: Overnight roadwork noted midweek MM 43–45 SB; no standing full closure. Check 511PA.
  • Transit: No new SCTA / rabbittransit / CAT capital award in this window. Statewide 2026–27 budget (signed July) did not add a large new transit package.

FMCSA / trucking & freight risk

  • HOS waiver (Sept. 16, 90 days): FMCSA lets gasoline/diesel drivers run up to 16 hours in a 24-hour window if they take required rest. Carriers with a conditional rating or active OOS order are excluded; incidents must be reported in two business days. Credit/ops: extra fuel-haul capacity through fall; only clean-safety-rated carriers can use it.
  • ELP / OOS NPRM (published Aug. 10): Would write English-language proficiency into FMCSRs as an out-of-service item, matching CVSA criteria. Comments due 60 days after publication. Credit/ops: higher roadside OOS risk and possible driver shortages on I-81/I-83/US-30 if adopted.
  • No new PA MCSAP blitz results specific to these four counties this week. PSP Labor Day weekend stats (Sept. 4–7) were statewide, not CMV-specific.

Cross-county / Harrisburg items that hit the region

Data-center siting and who pays for grid upgrades is the shared political and industrial theme: Lancaster dropped a moratorium for a task force; Smucker backed the House ratepayer bill; West Lebanon raised water-capacity questions. Farmland preservation continues in Lancaster (Colerain easement; West Donegal rezoning petition). I-81 overnight work next week will slow trucking between Carlisle and Harrisburg.

Sources

item.title: The telematics gap that’s costing fleets money — ATRI just mapped it
item.content:encoded:
From Data to Decisions: Trucking’s Use of Telematics Data to Improve Performance . The industry has more data than ever. The problem is not collection. It is conversion.

Operating costs excluding fuel are up 39% since 2020. Freight volumes have been flat. Deadhead, dwell, and miles between breakdowns have gotten worse. Telematics was supposed to help fleets fight that. Many still treat it like a compliance tool instead of a performance system.

Safety is table stakes. Everything else is lagging.

ATRI surveyed 111 carriers across fleet sizes (median 92 trucks, mean 1,910). They scored 44 KPIs on importance and actual use.

The top 10 “industry KPIs” — the ones that are both highly important and widely used — are all safety metrics:

  1. Critical events
  2. Speeding
  3. Risky driving behavior/trends
  4. Hard braking
  5. Driver distraction
  6. Behavior changes over time (coaching effectiveness)
  7. Positive driving behavior
  8. Crash rates
  9. Missed DVIRs
  10. Sudden lane departures

Four of those (critical events, speeding, hard braking, harsh turning) are used by more than 90% of respondents. Safety telematics is mature. That is not where the next dollar of value is sitting.

The real opportunity is in the metrics fleets rate high but do not use

ATRI calculated an “opportunity gap”: high-importance KPIs multiplied by the share of fleets not using them. The top 10 gaps:

  • Missed preventative maintenance (Maintenance)
  • Engine health (Maintenance)
  • Rollover risk indicators (Safety)
  • Cost per mile (Operations)
  • Defect/fault diagnostics (Maintenance)
  • Near-miss rates (Safety)
  • Crash rates (Safety)
  • Preventative maintenance scheduling (Maintenance)
  • Seatbelt compliance (Safety)
  • Driver distraction (Safety)

Cost per mile is the highest-rated operations KPI among users. Only 73% actually track it. That number should stop every operation and finance meeting. You cannot know if a lane or a customer is profitable if you do not know your true cost per mile.

Nearly half of fleets (48%) do not integrate telematics with maintenance management software. The most-used maintenance KPI — preventative maintenance scheduling — is still only at 77.5% utilization. That is lower than almost every safety metric.

Why the gap exists

Three consistent patterns in the report:

  • Larger fleets integrate telematics with TMS and maintenance systems far more often. Smaller fleets still dispatch by phone or text and run the numbers in spreadsheets.
  • Organizational silos and “data overload” are real. Providers told ATRI that fleets need people who can think like a data analyst and a trucker. The tools alone are not enough.
  • ROI skepticism still slows investment, especially when the benefits are harder to quantify than a speeding alert.

Fuel use/MPG and idle/dwell time are widely used. Cost per mile, engine health, and missed PM are not. That mismatch is expensive.

What this means if you run or insure a fleet

Safety scores and harsh-event coaching still matter. They reduce claims frequency and keep CSA numbers from becoming a commercial problem. But the next layer of performance — the one that protects cash flow — lives in maintenance and cost discipline.

A fleet that catches missed PMs, tracks engine health, and knows it's true cost per mile has fewer roadside breakdowns, less detention leakage, and cleaner books. Those are the same variables that show up in trade credit conversations: reliability, claims history, and the ability to stay current with vendors and lenders.

The report is a useful benchmark. If your fleet is already strong on critical events and speeding, the question is no longer “Do we have telematics?” It is “Which high-importance metric are we still leaving on the table?”

Which KPI on that opportunity-gap list is your fleet tracking well — and which one is still sitting unused?

item.title: The DOT tax — lost profit, compounded
item.content:encoded:
Forty-eight motor carriers in the lower Susquehanna Valley in the last twenty-four months read like a tax return nobody filed.

215 reportable crashes. 1 fatal. 75 injury. 139 tow-away. 387 times, a roadside inspector put a truck or a driver out of service. That is not a safety lecture. That is a P&L.

Call it the DOT tax. It is the money that leaves the account when a crash is litigated, when a unit sits, when CSA scores fall into the yellow or red. Those events are a loadstone around the neck of these companies. The expected bill across these fleets is $62.9M a year — 13.1% of estimated revenue. Cash already leaking before a jury is seated is $12.6M: deductibles, out-of-service downtime, and the commercial auto surcharge.

ATRI’s December 2025 forensic analysis of trucking litigation put the national median tractor-trailer award at $1.3M. A fatality raises that number by roughly 380 percent. The median nuclear verdict sits at $36.0M. Pennsylvania operations run toward Philadelphia, ATRA’s fifth Judicial Hellhole for 2025–26. FMCSA’s $750k minimum is a compliance number. It is not a survival number. 18 of these 48 fleets still file under $1.0M auto liability.

Every $165k of DOT tax is a truck that never made it to the yard.

Even at a 5 percent operating margin, every dollar of that tax costs twenty dollars of freight they have to go earn just to stand still. $62.9M of DOT tax is $1.3B of extra freight. At $165k, the number an owner can see from the window is simpler: 381 trucks this money could have purchased.

What could $62.9M have done for these companies?

The largest file on the snapshot accounts for 83 of those trucks — 46 reportable crashes, $13.7M a year, a $5.0M filing against a $36.0M median nuclear. A second fleet, with a fatality on the file, accounts for 56 more. Its crash rate sits well above the FMCSA peer of 4.77 per 100 power units. These are not hypotheticals. They are the last twenty-four months on the snapshot.

Cut the tax 20 percent — not a perfect year, a hiring-and-PM-and-HOS year — and these fleets get 76 trucks back. Or a retention check for the drivers who would have left. Or the working capital that funds the deductible and the next load. They pick one. That is the point. The procedures pay for the cash flow.

Compounded by the load that never moved

Lost revenue is the revenue already earned on the invoice. The DOT tax is the crash that already happened. Lost opportunity is the freight that never hit the dispatch board because the truck was not available — sitting at a scale, sitting in a shop, sitting in a lawyer’s file — or because a shipper looked at the CSA scorecard and sent the bid somewhere else because the same checking account that pays the claim is the one the grocer is waiting on.

NACM’s Credit Managers’ Index has said for years that firms which cannot see the buyer decline 5 to 12 percent of new-buyer applications. This model uses the floor: 6 percent of for-hire turnover, 4 percent of private product sales. In this snapshot, dairy, grain, ready-mix, and environmental fleets do not have to haul for hire to have a credit problem. They sell on terms. The lost opportunity is that the dealer will not put it on net-30.

Post-Montgomery, a thin certificate is not due diligence. Systems are the product.

The file is the product

On May 14, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 9–0 in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II. Freight brokers can be sued under state law for negligent carrier selection. The federal preemption defense that had kept the middle of the load board out of the courtroom is gone. A Dallas jury verdict against a major broker this summer made the forecast a number. Brokers will not tender into a file they cannot defend. Shippers will not either.

Auto is the policy. After Montgomery, the product is the system: hiring files, hours-of-service, preventative maintenance, cameras, CSA discipline — the due diligence that keeps trucks available and keeps the selection file from becoming Exhibit A. Improper hiring raises awards by 272 percent in ATRI’s forensic work. Employer negligence appears in 39 percent of nuclear cases. Hours of service, when alleged, show up in 75 percent of them. Fatigue, 63 percent. Those are not coverage questions. They are procedural questions. They are also why the truck was not available for the load that would have paid for the procedure.

The practical next step is to put last year’s crashes on one page with published unit costs, ask what they actually cost, and ask how many trucks the owner wants back. Then ask which units sat last quarter and whether a broker pulling the CSA and hiring file tonight would still tender the load.

48 companies. 215 crashes. 387 out-of-service events. 381 trucks that never made the yard. The DOT tax is lost profit. Lost opportunity is the compound. Credit and cash flow are how they say yes when the unit is finally available. Systems and due diligence are what keep it that way.

Crash and inspection counts are from Central Analysis Bureau snapshots of forty-eight motor carriers in the lower Susquehanna Valley, 2–3 September 2026. Unit costs cite ATRI, Trucking Litigation: A Forensic Analysis (December 2025), FMCSA, and NHTSA. Revenue, A/R, and lost-opportunity figures are modeled from MCS-150 mileage and fleet mix — estimates, not audited financials. Nuclear-verdict medians cite ATRI 2025. Judicial Hellhole ranking: ATRA 2025–26.

I am always open to a conversation; let's work through this together.

item.title: After Montgomery, Hope Is Not a Defense
item.content:encoded:
Freight operators are being squeezed from three sides at once: legal exposure after the Supreme Court’s Montgomery ruling, insurance costs that are no longer a rounding error, and a market where capacity is tightening while inventory and warehouse costs stay high. For CEOs, CFOs, controllers, and credit managers, this is not an abstract legal story. It is a cashflow, balance-sheet, and customer-solvency story.

When money is cheap, weak underwriting hides. When the cost of money stays high and juries keep writing large checks, every loose process — carrier selection, overflow brokerage, and open-account sales — shows up on the P&L. The firms that document risk and protect receivables will keep growing. The ones that rely on “we always use good brokers” will find that phrase does not survive cross-examination.

⚖️ Montgomery Changed the Rulebook. Insurance Is Pricing It.

•  The May 2026 Montgomery decision removed the federal preemption shield brokers had used to knock out negligent-selection suits early. Brokers can now be sued in state court for the carriers they put on the road.

•  Underwriters are reacting in the only language they speak price and capacity. TD Cowen reported a top 10 broker seeing liability coverage triple at renewal. Large-broker rate increases are landing in the mid-teens to mid-20s. Excess layers above $5 million are seeing 50% to triple-digit jumps.

•  The supply of paper is shrinking. Only about ten underwriters still write broker auto liability, and that number is expected to fall. Two markets have already stepped back. Fewer sellers plus larger verdicts is not a temporary spike. It is a new cost of doing business.

•  For shippers and 3PLs, that premium inflation does not stay on the broker’s books. It lands in rates, in tighter carrier lists, and in slower payment when a mid-size broker’s working capital is consumed by insurance instead of growth.

🚛 Penske Fallout: Liability Is Traveling Up the Chain

•  ATA and TCA have asked the full Fifth Circuit to rehear a ruling that put Penske Logistics on the hook for a fatal crash involving a double-brokered driver the company says it did not know. The associations warn the decision could rewrite how carrier liability attaches when freight is tendered downstream.

•  The practical message is simple. Handing a load to the next party in the chain no longer reliably ends your exposure. Asset-based carriers that also broker, private fleets that overflow to for-hire capacity, and 3PLs that double-broker are all in the same photograph.

•  If your private fleet cannot cover a load and dispatch calls outside, “it depends who is on shift” is not a standard. In a post-Montgomery courtroom, an undocumented overflow process is a plaintiff’s exhibit.

📉 Small Carriers Face a Narrower Door

•  Two leading transportation attorneys put it plainly: this may not be the right time to jump into the small-carrier market. Brokers are writing stricter selection policies. Conditional carriers and new authorities are losing freight first.

•  Insurance costs, rising minimums, and fewer brokers willing to tender to a five-truck fleet are already pushing independents toward larger authorities. Scale is becoming a safety credential as much as a cost advantage.

•  That consolidation changes credit risk for everyone upstream. When a small carrier or mid-size broker exits, unpaid freight bills and stranded loads show up as AR write-offs for shippers and as claim files for anyone who extended terms.

🔎 The Roadside Crackdown Is a Capacity and Credit Event

•  Federal and state enforcement on CDL mills, English-language proficiency, and non-domiciled licenses has pulled tens of thousands of drivers and thousands of training schools out of the system. A new interagency fraud push announced at the end of August widens the net.

•  Cleaner roads are the stated goal. The side effect is a thinner, more expensive driver pool. Firms that hired fast and cheap now carry both compliance risk and customer-concentration risk if those drivers disappear.

•  Policy that favors connected, well-capitalized operators over thin-margin independents is not new. What is new is how quickly that preference is showing up in insurance pricing and in who still gets tendered freight.

📊 LMI Snapshot: Tight Capacity, Sticky Costs

•  The July Logistics Managers’ Index printed 68.9 — off June’s 71.1 high, but still stronger than any reading from 2023 through 2025. August eased further to 66.6. Expansion is slowing, not reversing.

•  Transportation capacity contracted to 28.4 in July, one of the fastest tightenings in the index’s history. Transportation prices stayed in very robust expansion (86.9). Warehouse capacity is also tight; inventory costs hit 77 even as inventory growth cooled.

•  That mix — expensive freight, expensive storage, and slower inventory builds — is hard on working capital. When the currency of growth is credit and cash conversion, a late-paying customer or a failed broker is not a sales problem. It is a solvency problem.

Final Thought

The industry is being repriced around documented care: who you put on the road, who you overflow to, and who you sell on open account. Protection is not the opposite of growth. It is what lets a trucking company, 3PL, or shipper keep selling when the legal and insurance environment stops subsidizing sloppy selection. Accounts receivable remains the largest uninsured asset on most freight balance sheets. Treat them with the same discipline now required for carrier vetting.

If you run a private fleet with overflow capacity, a brokerage, or a carrier network that still sells on terms, I am glad to walk through how your current process would look under cross-examination — and how trade credit insurance and structured risk tools can protect AR, stabilize cash flow, and support safer sales growth.
