item.title: Broker Liability Reset and Oil Supply Shock: New Risks Reshaping Freight Economics
item.content:encoded:
⚖️ SCOTUS Unanimously Opens Brokers to Negligent Hiring Suits

  • In Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC (decided May 14, 2026), the Supreme Court ruled 9-0 that state-law negligent-hiring claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (FAAAA).
  • The Court held that such claims fall within the FAAAA’s safety exception, preserving state authority “with respect to motor vehicles.” Justice Amy Coney Barrett’s opinion made clear that requiring ordinary care in selecting a carrier concerns the trucks that move the freight.
  • The decision resolves a circuit split and allows injured parties to pursue brokers in state court when a carrier involved in a crash had known safety deficiencies (such as a conditional FMCSA rating).

Trucking & logistics relevance: Every carrier selection decision is now potentially discoverable evidence. Plaintiff counsel will focus on whether a meaningful vetting process existed and whether it was actually followed on the specific load.

📋 “The Vetting Process Is Now the Product”

  • Industry observers note that a written policy alone is no longer enough. Defense counsel are advising that the process itself has become the product: documented, load-level records of authority checks, insurance verification, safety data review, exception approvals, and continuous monitoring are essential.
  • Without contemporaneous proof that the standard was applied to the specific shipment, brokers face a binary risk: either no real process existed, or the process was not followed. Either path supports a negligence finding.
  • Recent jury activity and post-ruling appeals (including cases involving large logistics firms) show the practical impact is already materializing.

Insurance & risk angle: transportation and logistics, along with their insurers, face higher litigation frequency and severity. Documented, consistent carrier selection is now both a legal defense and an underwriting signal. Gaps in process create direct exposure that can cascade into higher insurance costs and strained counterparty relationships.

🛢️ Crude Markets Face Impending Supply Tightness

  • Maritime intelligence firm Vortexa reports a simultaneous collapse in seaborne crude exports from Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and the United States, driving the combined volume to a record low. Over four weeks, crude oil on the water drew down at more than 7 million barrels per day—nearly twice the pace seen earlier in the year.
  • Iran’s flows were hit by the re-imposition of a U.S. blockade near the Strait of Hormuz; Saudi exports faced Gulf and Red Sea tensions; Russian exports suffered from Black Sea infrastructure attacks; and U.S. exports eased amid slower strategic reserve releases and weak arbitrage to Asia.
  • Analysts describe the mid-July appearance of ample supply as a “false dawn.” Prices are viewed as undervalued relative to physical data, with inventory draws and geopolitical risk supporting higher risk premiums. Sanctions-evasion activity (including high-risk vessel clusters near the Strait) adds further complexity.

Supply-chain relevance: Fuel is a major variable cost for trucking and logistics. Tightness and volatility feed directly into rate pressure, capacity decisions, and the financial health of carriers and shippers. SMEs with concentrated customer or supplier exposure face amplified working-capital risk when energy costs spike or counterparties strain under higher operating expenses.

Framing the Bigger Picture

Policy choices and concentrated interests continue to shape both the legal rules governing liability allocation and the physical constraints on energy supply. When federal preemption narrows, and key commodity export channels tighten at the same time, the result is higher uncertainty, higher compliance and insurance costs, and greater potential for payment delays or defaults further down the chain. Companies that treat risk management as a series of isolated silos (legal, insurance, credit, operations) leave gaps that volatility exploits.

Final Thought: In an environment where a single carrier selection decision can become courtroom evidence and fuel markets can tighten faster than models predicted, fragmented risk approaches leave working capital exposed. Integrated 360-degree risk management—combining traditional commercial insurance lines with tools that protect accounts receivable and support resilient cash flow—helps SMEs in trucking, logistics, manufacturing, and distribution stay solvent and competitive when the unexpected arrives.

I’m happy to share practical insights on Trade Credit Insurance (TCI), Supply Chain Finance (SCF), and a full-spectrum approach to protecting your business.

item.title: Every carrier selection is a decision that must be able to stand on its own in a deposition or trial: Carrier Vetting Is Now the Product
item.content:encoded:
Introduction On May 14, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC that the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (FAAAA) does not shield freight brokers from state-law negligent-hiring claims. The decision resolves a multi-circuit split and removes a long-relied-upon federal defense. In an environment already strained by elevated liability costs, insurance market hardening, and operational pressures, this ruling makes every carrier selection decision a potential exhibit—and elevates the need for disciplined risk management across trucking, brokerage, and logistics.

🚛 What the Court Actually Decided

  • Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for a 9-0 Court. The FAAAA preempts state laws related to a broker’s price, route, or service, but the statute’s safety exception preserves state authority to regulate safety “with respect to motor vehicles.”
  • A claim that a broker negligently selected an unsafe motor carrier concerns the trucks that will operate on public roads and therefore falls within the safety exception.
  • The case stemmed from a 2017 Illinois crash in which driver Shawn Montgomery suffered catastrophic injuries (including leg amputation) after being struck by a Caribe Transport truck that C.H. Robinson had brokered. Caribe carried a conditional safety rating.
  • The ruling reverses the Seventh Circuit and aligns the law nationwide: brokers can no longer obtain early dismissal of these claims solely on FAAAA preemption grounds.

Vetting Is Now the Product—and Documentation Is the Defense: Norris Beren, founder of Risk Reward Consulting and creator of the Case Dismissed Protocol, put it plainly in a post-Montgomery analysis: a written vetting policy is only the first layer. The second—and decisive—layer is the ability to prove that the policy was actually followed for the specific load on the specific date.

As Beren notes, one transportation defense firm told its broker clients after the ruling that “the vetting process is now the product, and every carrier selection decision is a potential exhibit.” Plaintiff’s counsel is working toward one of two conclusions in discovery: either no meaningful process existed, or a process existed and was not followed. Either finding supports a negligence claim.

This is the essence of controlling the controllables. Brokers cannot control the weather, traffic, or a driver’s split-second decision. They can control whether they have a clear standard, whether they apply it consistently, and whether they can produce a dated, retrievable record of what was checked and decided before the truck rolled.

Where controlling the controllables has paid off (and where the absence of it hurts)

  • Brokers who maintain contemporaneous, timestamped records—SAFER snapshot at the moment of selection, BASIC percentiles reviewed, insurance verification, red-flag notes, and documented exception approvals—are positioned to show a jury they exercised ordinary care. Multiple post-Montgomery analyses (including Justice Kavanaugh’s concurrence) emphasize that brokers who “ask the hard questions” and can demonstrate what they knew at the time of selection face a markedly stronger defense posture.
  • Conversely, brokers who rely on a policy that lives only in a binder or an onboarding checklist, without load-level proof of execution, hand plaintiffs the narrative that the process was either nonexistent or ignored. That gap has already become the central focus of discovery in the first wave of cases.
  • Practical examples of the payoff appear in the operational shifts underway: large brokers tightening acceptance thresholds and removing higher-risk carriers from boards shortly after the ruling, and technology platforms that automatically capture the selection record becoming standard risk-management tools. The brokers building these contemporaneous files now are the ones who will be able to produce them years later when a subpoena arrives—turning what could have been an indefensible claim into a defensible one.

In short, the strategy that works is not merely having a policy. It treats every carrier selection as a decision that must stand on its own in a deposition or trial. That is fully within a broker’s control. The operators who treat it as such are already separating themselves from those still operating under the old preemption mindset.

(The rest of the newsletter remains unchanged, with the Final Thought and CTA continuing to position rigorous operational controls plus TCI/SCF as complementary layers of 360-degree risk management.)

⚖️ Practical Ripple Effects Across the Chain

  • Brokers face heightened exposure and must audit selection criteria, tighten hard stops for conditional or unsatisfactory ratings, strengthen monitoring for fraud and double-brokering, and confirm that liability coverage responds to negligent-selection claims.
  • Carriers with weaker safety profiles will find it harder to obtain freight; those with clean records and documented programs become more valuable.
  • Shippers should expect revised contract language around carrier selection standards, indemnification, and insurance requirements, and should document their own expectations of broker partners.
  • Insurance markets and underwriters are already reassessing broker accounts. Claims volume for negligent-hiring filings is expected to rise.

These pressures do not exist in isolation. When institutional and policy choices increase the cost and complexity of liability, operators across freight and logistics face tighter margins, higher insurance costs, and greater strain on working capital—exactly the conditions under which unprotected accounts receivable and counterparty exposure become acute.

Final Thought: Montgomery does not invent a new duty of ordinary care; it removes the federal procedural shield that had blocked state courts from enforcing it against brokers. Responsible operators who already maintain rigorous, documented selection processes gain a competitive and defensive advantage. Those who treat carrier selection as a low-friction transactional step now face a different legal and commercial reality. In this environment, 360-degree risk management—combining strong operational controls with tools that protect cash flow and mitigate counterparty default—is no longer optional for sustainable growth.

Call to Action: If your brokerage, carrier operation, or shipper network is assessing post-Montgomery exposure, carrier-selection protocols, insurance implications, or broader working-capital protection, I am available to discuss practical approaches. Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) and Supply Chain Finance (SCF) remain essential tools for protecting accounts receivable and supporting growth amid elevated legal and operational risk.

item.title: 🚚💰 Why Accounts Receivable Are Becoming More Valuable Than Ever
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

A major shift is happening in business lending.

Banks, private lenders, and investors still have money to lend, but they are becoming more selective about where that money goes. Today, lenders care less about revenue growth alone and more about cash flow quality, customer risk, and the strength of a company's accounts receivable.

For trucking companies, freight brokers, third-party logistics providers (3PLs), manufacturers, wholesalers, and distributors, this trend creates both challenges and opportunities.

The companies that can demonstrate strong receivables, predictable cash flow, and disciplined credit management are often in a better position to access capital and support growth.

🏦 The Rise of Asset-Based Lending (ABL)

What is Asset-Based Lending?

Asset-Based Lending (ABL) is a loan secured by company assets rather than relying solely on company profits.

Common examples of collateral include:

  • Accounts receivable (customer invoices)
  • Inventory
  • Equipment
  • Trucks and trailers
  • Warehouses
  • Machinery

Why It Matters

Lenders are increasingly looking at the quality of assets behind a loan.

For many businesses, accounts receivable represents the largest asset on the balance sheet.

When lenders evaluate an Accounts Receivable (A/R) portfolio, they typically ask:

  • Are customers paying on time?
  • How concentrated are sales among a few large customers?
  • How financially strong are those customers?
  • How much bad debt risk exists?

The stronger the receivables, the more attractive the borrower becomes.

Transportation & Logistics Relevance

For carriers, brokers, and logistics providers, receivables generated from freight movements are becoming increasingly valuable financing assets.

Quality receivables can support:

  • Working capital facilities
  • Asset-based lines of credit
  • Receivables financing programs
  • Growth initiatives

⛽ Understanding Reserve-Based Lending (RBL)

What is Reserve-Based Lending?

Reserve-Based Lending (RBL) is a specialized lending structure commonly used in energy industries.

Unlike ABL, which uses existing assets as collateral, RBL loans are based on the expected future value of assets that will produce cash flow over time.

Examples include:

  • Oil reserves
  • Natural gas reserves
  • Mining assets

Why Trucking Companies Should Care

Most trucking companies will never use Reserve-Based Lending directly.

However, RBL highlights a broader trend:

Investors increasingly want loans backed by identifiable assets and predictable cash flows.

That same philosophy is now being applied to:

  • Freight receivables
  • Fleet assets
  • Transportation contracts
  • Warehouse assets

Recent energy finance discussions show continued investor demand for Asset-Backed Securities (ABS) and Reserve-Based Lending structures, while also emphasizing the importance of risk management and underwriting discipline. 📈 Private Credit Continues To Expand

What is Private Credit?

Private credit refers to loans made by non-bank lenders instead of traditional banks.

Examples include:

  • Blackstone
  • Apollo
  • Ares
  • Blue Owl

Private credit has expanded dramatically over the last two decades and has become a major source of business financing. The Financial Stability Board estimates private credit grew from approximately $40 billion in 2000 to approximately $2.3 trillion by the end of 2025.

Key Trends

Growth areas include:

  • Direct lending
  • Asset-based finance
  • Receivables financing
  • Infrastructure debt
  • Specialty lending

Many of these lenders are heavily focused on collateral quality and cash flow predictability.

Transportation & Logistics Relevance

This means trucking and logistics companies now have more financing options than ever before.

However, those financing options increasingly depend on:

  • Receivable quality
  • Customer diversification
  • Collection performance
  • Credit discipline

⚠️ What Lenders Are Paying Attention To

Middle-market companies continue facing pressure from:

  • Higher borrowing costs
  • Wage inflation
  • Rising operating expenses
  • Competitive pricing pressure

As a result, lenders and investors are placing greater emphasis on:

Accounts Receivable Quality

Are invoices collectible?

Customer Concentration Risk

Does one customer represent too much revenue?

Collections Performance

How quickly are invoices converted into cash?

Customer Creditworthiness

Can customers actually pay?

Liquidity Planning

Can the company survive unexpected payment delays?

These topics are becoming central to credit decisions across both banking and private credit markets.

💵 Cash Flow Quality Matters

Whether capital comes from:

  • Banks
  • Asset-Based Lenders
  • Private Credit Funds
  • Institutional Investors

The questions remain largely the same:

  • Are customers paying on time?
  • How concentrated is customer risk?
  • What is the probability of bad debt?
  • Is cash flow consistent?
  • Is working capital managed effectively?

For many companies in transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and wholesale distribution, accounts receivable is often the largest uninsured asset on the balance sheet.

🛡️ Why Trade Credit Insurance Matters

Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) helps protect businesses when customers:

  • Become insolvent
  • File bankruptcy
  • Fail to pay

As lenders focus more heavily on receivables quality, Trade Credit Insurance becomes more than an insurance product.

It can help companies:

✅ Protect cash flow

✅ Reduce bad debt exposure

✅ Extend credit more confidently

✅ Support growth into new customers and markets

✅ Strengthen financing conversations

✅ Improve working capital management

Final Thought

The message coming from banks, private lenders, investors, and regulators is remarkably consistent:

Companies with predictable cash flow, strong receivables, disciplined credit management, and effective risk controls are becoming more attractive borrowers.

For trucking companies, freight brokers, logistics providers, manufacturers, wholesalers, and distributors, managing receivables risk is no longer just a credit function.

It is becoming a growth strategy.

item.title: 🚛 Broker Liability, Nuclear Verdicts & The New Freight Risk Reality
item.content:encoded:
The transportation industry is entering a new era of legal and operational risk. Recent court decisions, evolving carrier vetting expectations, and growing concerns around nuclear verdicts are reshaping how freight brokers, carriers, shippers, and insurers manage exposure.

The message is becoming clear: documentation, defensible processes, and proactive risk management are no longer optional. They are becoming critical competitive advantages.

⚖️ Montgomery v. Caribe: The Liability Landscape Has Changed

The U.S. Supreme Court's Montgomery v. Caribe Transport decision has significantly altered the broker liability discussion. The Court held that negligent hiring and negligent selection claims against brokers may proceed under state law through the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (FAAAA) safety exception.

Key Takeaways

  • Brokers can no longer rely on Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act preemption as an automatic early dismissal strategy in negligent selection cases.
  • Plaintiffs now have a clearer pathway to pursue claims alleging a broker failed to use reasonable care when selecting a motor carrier.
  • The Court emphasized this is not strict liability. Plaintiffs still must prove the broker failed to exercise ordinary care.
  • Industry attorneys warn that even when brokers ultimately prevail, litigation costs, discovery demands, and settlement pressure may increase substantially.

Why It Matters

For freight brokers, third-party logistics providers (3PLs), trucking companies, and insurers, the focus shifts from simply meeting minimum compliance standards to demonstrating a documented and repeatable carrier vetting process. The ability to explain decisions may become as important as the decisions themselves.

🔎 What Plaintiff Attorneys Are Looking for Now

A recent FreightWaves interview with plaintiff attorney Michael Leizerman and transportation legal expert Cassandra Gaines outlined the factors increasingly attracting scrutiny after serious crashes.

Common Red Flags

  • Conditional safety ratings.
  • Newly authorized carriers with limited operating history.
  • Chameleon carriers and authority manipulation concerns.
  • Stolen authority and identity mismatches.
  • Elevated out-of-service rates.
  • Repeated involuntary revocations.
  • Lack of written vetting procedures.
  • Missing documentation explaining carrier selection decisions.

Why It Matters

The industry conversation is moving beyond "Did you check insurance?" to "Can you demonstrate a reasonable and consistent process?" This creates greater demand for technology, documentation, continuous monitoring, and governance controls.

From a broader financial perspective, whenever liability exposures become harder to quantify, capital providers, insurers, and lenders often demand higher premiums, larger reserves, and tighter underwriting standards. Those costs ultimately work their way through transportation pricing and supply chains.

💰 The Rise of Nuclear Verdict Risk

Industry leaders continue to express concerns regarding the growth of large jury awards and litigation financing.

According to the American Trucking Associations, trucking companies face increasing pressure from:

  • Direct negligence claims.
  • Third-party litigation finance.
  • Forum shopping.
  • Phantom damages.
  • Expanding non-economic damage awards.

Key Concerns

  • Eight- and nine-figure verdicts can threaten carrier solvency and increase industry insurance costs.
  • Higher legal exposure may increase operating costs across the supply chain.
  • Insurers are expected to place increased emphasis on underwriting quality, carrier selection, and risk controls.

Why It Matters

Whether one views these developments as necessary accountability or excessive litigation, the practical effect is the same: risk management has become a boardroom issue, not merely a safety department issue.

🛡️ Insurance, Contracts & Risk Management Are Becoming Strategic Weapons

There are three major impact zones resulting from the Montgomery decision:

1️⃣ Litigation

  • Increased likelihood brokers will be named defendants.
  • Expanded discovery requests.
  • Greater settlement pressure before trial.

2️⃣ Contractual Risk Transfer

  • More aggressive indemnification negotiations.
  • Increased demand for additional insured status.
  • Greater focus on certificates of insurance and coverage verification.
  • Stronger carrier onboarding requirements.

3️⃣ Insurance Market Response

  • Potential premium increases.
  • Broader differences in policy wording.
  • Increased importance of transportation-focused insurance expertise.
  • Greater emphasis on documented carrier vetting standards.

Why It Matters

Organizations that treat risk management as a process rather than a paperwork exercise will likely be better positioned to defend claims, maintain insurability, and preserve customer relationships.

💡 Lessons for Trade Credit Insurance & Business Risk Management

While the headlines focus on trucking liability, the underlying business lesson applies to every company extending credit, shipping goods, and managing customer relationships.

  • Risk rarely appears without warning.
  • Documentation often determines outcomes.
  • Strong vetting processes create resilience.
  • Insurance works best when paired with proactive risk management.

For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), risk management cannot be siloed. Nothing happens in a vacuum.

Financial pressure rarely stays confined to the balance sheet. Margin compression and cash flow stress can trigger a chain reaction across the business:

  • Deferred maintenance and longer equipment replacement cycles
  • Lower hiring standards or difficulty attracting experienced drivers
  • Taking on more freight than operations can comfortably support
  • Increased pressure on drivers, dispatchers, and maintenance teams
  • Greater reliance on debt to fund working capital and daily operations
  • Higher accident, breakdown, compliance, and liability exposure

What begins as a financial problem can quickly become an operational problem, a safety problem, and eventually a legal or insurance problem.

Final Thought

The transportation industry is moving toward a higher standard of defensibility. Whether evaluating carriers, customers, suppliers, or business partners, success increasingly belongs to organizations that can demonstrate disciplined decision-making and documented risk controls.

The companies that win in this environment will not necessarily be those taking the least risk. They will be the ones best prepared to explain and manage it.

item.title: 🔗 Blockchain, Smart Contracts & NFTs Could Become the Next Layer of Supply Chain Risk Management
item.content:encoded:
While most discussions around blockchain focus on cryptocurrency, the most practical transportation applications may be in freight documentation, cargo verification, carrier identity validation, and payment automation. Blockchain's ability to create tamper-resistant records and automate contractual actions through smart contracts is increasingly being explored across logistics and supply chains. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]

Why This Matters Now

Recent FreightWaves reporting highlights a growing concern for shippers:

The wrong truck arriving at the dock can now create significant liability risks. Verifying the carrier, DOT number, driver, and equipment before releasing freight is becoming increasingly important as fraud, rebrokering schemes, and identity issues gain greater legal scrutiny. [ freightwaves.com ]

The challenge is that most of today's freight documentation process still relies heavily on:

  • Emails
  • PDFs
  • Phone calls
  • Bills of lading
  • Manual carrier verification
  • Fragmented transportation management systems

Each creates an opportunity for error, fraud, or miscommunication.

🚚 Digital Freight Documentation Through NFTs

In logistics, Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs) are not digital artwork.

Instead, they can serve as unique digital representations of:

  • Bills of lading
  • Shipping containers
  • Cargo ownership records
  • Insurance certificates
  • Chain-of-custody documents

Each shipment could receive a unique digital identity that cannot be duplicated or altered after issuance. Blockchain-based tokenization creates a permanent record of every transfer, scan, handoff, and ownership change. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]

Potential Benefits

✅ Reduced document fraud

✅ Improved cargo visibility

✅ Faster dispute resolution

✅ Stronger chain-of-custody records

✅ Better carrier verification

🤖 Smart Contracts Could Automate Payment and Compliance

Smart contracts are self-executing agreements that automatically perform actions when predefined conditions are met. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]

Imagine a future workflow:

Shipment Created → Freight Escrow Funded → Delivery Verified → Payment Released Automatically

Potential Use Cases

  • Carrier payments released immediately upon verified delivery.
  • Cold-chain shipments automatically monitored through IoT sensors.
  • Insurance claims triggered automatically when shipment criteria are violated.
  • Customs documentation verified before cargo reaches borders.
  • Factoring and supply-chain-finance programs funded automatically once delivery milestones are met.

Instead of waiting 30, 60, or 90 days, payment could be tied directly to verified operational events. [ appinventiv.com ] , [ builtin.com ]

⚠️ The Trust Problem: Data Is Only as Good as Its Source

Blockchain eliminates document tampering.

It does not eliminate bad data.

The biggest challenge remains the "oracle problem."

If an IoT sensor, GPS device, RFID reader, or external data feed provides inaccurate information, a smart contract will execute based on incorrect inputs. [ appinventiv.com ]

Questions companies must still solve:

  • Was the carrier properly vetted?
  • Was the shipment actually delivered?
  • Was the sensor functioning correctly?
  • Did the cargo condition data accurately reflect reality?

Technology can improve trust, but it does not completely replace operational controls.

🛡️ Risk Management Meets Technology

The recent FreightWaves discussion regarding shipper liability illustrates why digital verification systems may become increasingly valuable. When a carrier's identity, DOT number, driver, or equipment does not match the approved assignment, companies need reliable verification procedures before freight is released. [ freightwaves.com ]

A future blockchain-enabled workflow could potentially create:

  • Verified carrier identities
  • Immutable pickup records
  • Real-time chain-of-custody documentation
  • Automated approval workflows
  • Digital proof of delivery

all available through a shared, auditable record. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]

💡 What you Should Be Watching

While widespread adoption remains in the early stages, several trends suggest momentum is building:

  • Tokenization of real-world assets continues growing. [ appinventiv.com ]
  • Smart contract adoption is expanding across industries. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]
  • Blockchain applications in logistics continue attracting enterprise investment. [ builtin.com ] , [ appinventiv.com ]
  • Ethereum network activity recently surged, indicating growing utilization of blockchain infrastructure despite volatile market conditions. [ cryptorank.io ]

The long-term opportunity may not be cryptocurrency itself.

The opportunity may be creating faster, safer, and more trustworthy supply chains.

🎯 Perspective

Whether blockchain becomes a dominant infrastructure layer or remains a specialized tool, the underlying business objective remains unchanged:

Trust.

Companies want confidence that:

  • The shipment is real.
  • The carrier is legitimate.
  • The documents are authentic.
  • The customer can pay.
  • The receivable will be collected.

Blockchain may eventually improve verification.

Trade credit insurance helps protect the balance sheet when verification alone is not enough.

After all, a perfectly authenticated receivable can still become a bad debt.

item.title: Trucking Risk & Capacity Outlook
item.content:encoded:
The trucking market is sending mixed signals. Freight demand remains uneven, but capacity has steadily exited the market after years of margin compression. At the same time, operating costs, insurance expenses, and financing pressures continue to rise. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

For shippers, carriers, brokers, lenders, and transportation service providers, this combination creates a new risk environment where protecting cash flow and evaluating counterparty strength becomes increasingly important.

🚛 Truck Capacity Shortage Is Emerging Again

A recent FreightWaves analysis highlights a developing capacity crunch as carriers continue to exit the market while freight demand begins to stabilize.

Key Takeaways

  • Capacity has been leaving the trucking market for multiple years. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Higher freight rates are increasingly being driven by reduced capacity rather than strong freight demand. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Smaller and financially weaker carriers remain vulnerable to rising costs and tightening liquidity. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Any meaningful demand rebound could create upward pricing pressure quickly. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Why It Matters

When capacity tightens, shippers often:

  • Extend more credit to customers.
  • Increase inventory commitments.
  • Face higher transportation costs.
  • Experience greater concentration risk with key carriers and customers.

From a risk management perspective, tighter capacity can improve carrier pricing power while simultaneously increasing working capital requirements throughout the supply chain.

📈 Operational Costs Continue Reaching New Records

According to the American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI), average trucking operating costs reached a record $2.336 per mile in 2025 , increasing 3.4% year over year. Excluding fuel, costs increased 4.2%. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Key Cost Drivers

  • Driver wages: $0.818 per mile [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Driver benefits: $0.210 per mile [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Insurance premiums: $0.106 per mile and continuing to rise [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Repair and maintenance costs increased 8.6% year over year [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Toll costs increased 13.2% year over year [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Why It Matters

Many carriers remain under significant financial pressure.

Warning signs often include:

  • Slower vendor payments
  • Increased leverage
  • Delayed equipment replacement
  • Reduced fleet investment
  • Greater credit risk exposure

Monitoring customer, supplier, and carrier financial strength is becoming increasingly important for both transportation providers and freight buyers.

💰 Capacity Recovery Is Being Driven by Supply Reduction, Not Demand Growth

ATRI's latest research suggests freight rate improvements are being driven primarily by capacity leaving the market rather than a major increase in freight demand. Effective trucking capacity declined materially as fleets reduced truck counts and parked equipment. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Key Observations

  • Returning fleets reduced capacity during 2025. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Approximately 10% of trucks were unseated or parked. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Freight rates improved while freight volumes remained mixed. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Effective capacity declined by an estimated 5.5% during 2025. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Broader Economic Context

Long-term fiscal imbalances and expanding public debt can create uncertainty around inflation, financing costs, and capital allocation decisions. Historical experience suggests that sustainable growth ultimately depends on productive economic activity rather than relying indefinitely on low borrowing costs. [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]

Businesses should therefore remain focused on:

  • Balance sheet strength
  • Liquidity management
  • Working capital efficiency
  • Customer credit quality
  • Counterparty risk monitoring

rather than assuming favorable financing conditions will persist indefinitely. [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]

⚖️ Insurance Costs Remain a Major Industry Challenge

Truck insurance costs continue to rise despite improvements in safety performance. ATRI reports insurance premiums increased 3.9% during 2025 and continued rising into early 2026. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Key Trends

  • Litigation costs remain elevated. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Total cost of risk continues increasing. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Large fleets are increasingly exploring alternative risk-transfer strategies. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Insurance renewals continue experiencing upward pricing pressure. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

Why It Matters

A carrier's insurance strategy increasingly reflects its overall financial health.

Companies that proactively manage:

  • Safety
  • Credit risk
  • Loss prevention
  • Liquidity
  • Cash flow

often outperform competitors during challenging freight cycles. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

🏦 What This Means for Credit, Cash Flow, and Growth

As supply chains adjust to tighter capacity and rising costs, many businesses face a common challenge:

How do you continue growing sales while controlling payment risk?

Key Questions Executives Should Be Asking

  • Are key customers financially healthy enough to absorb higher transportation costs?
  • Are receivables becoming more concentrated?
  • Are suppliers or carriers under increasing financial stress?
  • Can working capital support growth if payment terms lengthen?
  • What happens if a top customer suddenly defaults?

Strong organizations increasingly view accounts receivable as a strategic asset deserving the same level of protection and monitoring as physical assets or inventory.

💸 The Hidden Cost of a Customer Default

Many companies focus on revenue growth, but few calculate how much new revenue is required to recover from a bad debt loss.

When margins are thin, a single unpaid invoice can erase the profit from dozens of successful shipments.

Revenue Required to Recover a $100,000 Bad Debt Loss

Net Profit Margin Revenue Needed

1% $10,000,000

2% $5,000,000

5% $2,000,000

10% $1,000,000

20% $500,000

Source: Revenue recovery analysis. [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]

Real-World Example

If a transportation company suffers a $100,000 customer default :

  • At a 5% profit margin , it must generate $2 million in additional sales to recover the loss. [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]
  • At a 2% profit margin , it needs $5 million in additional sales . [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]
  • At a 1% profit margin , it must generate $10 million in new revenue just to break even. [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]

In an industry where many trucking operators are earning margins below 5%, protecting receivables can be just as important as winning new freight. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF] , [revenue_margin_grid | Excel]

Why It Matters for Transportation Companies

  • Freight remains cyclical. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Capacity reductions are supporting rates, but demand growth remains uneven. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • Cash flow remains under pressure from rising insurance, equipment, labor, maintenance, and financing costs. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]
  • A single bankruptcy or non-payment event can erase an entire year's profit.

The difference between an uninsured receivable and a protected receivable is often measured in millions of dollars of replacement revenue.

🎯 Final Thought

The trucking market appears to be transitioning from a freight recession toward a tightening-capacity environment. Improving rates are encouraging, but rising operating costs, elevated insurance expenses, litigation exposure, and growing counterparty risk remain significant challenges. [John H.Cochrane∗ | PDF]

As capacity tightens and financial pressures persist, the strongest companies will not simply focus on moving more freight. They will focus on protecting cash flow, strengthening working capital, monitoring customer risk, and preventing losses before they occur.

In today's market, growth is important.

Getting paid may be even more important.

item.title: Sound Public Credit & Supply Chain Resilience: Lessons on Debt, Fiscal Discipline, and Credit Risk for Trucking SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Government debt levels and the credibility of repayment plans are no longer abstract policy debates. They directly influence the cost of fuel, equipment financing, customer solvency, and working capital across the trucking and logistics sectors. Recent discussions revisiting Alexander Hamilton’s 1790 First Report on Public Credit alongside contemporary analysis of fiscal policy’s role in price determination deliver timely reminders: when governments credibly commit to honoring and eventually retiring their obligations, the result is greater confidence, lower borrowing costs, and more predictable conditions for commerce. SMEs moving freight feel these effects in real time through interest rates, input costs, and the creditworthiness of their customers.

📜 Hamilton’s Blueprint: Funding Debt to Build Confidence and Commerce

Alexander Hamilton’s landmark report established the principles that turned a fractured post-war debt burden into a foundation for national credit and economic expansion. His core recommendations included funding the federal debt at full value, assuming state debts on equal terms, creating a sinking fund to retire principal over time, and refusing to discriminate between original creditors and later purchasers.

  • Full funding and assumption of debts unified creditor interests, eliminated destructive competition for revenues between levels of government, and restored faith that the United States would meet its obligations.
  • The sinking fund mechanism paired new debt creation with a concrete, revenue-backed plan for eventual repayment—embedding the maxim that sustainable credit requires a visible path to extinguishment.
  • Equal treatment of all holders' upheld contracts, prevented arbitrary redistribution, and allowed funded debt to function as a stable, money-like instrument that circulated in trade and supported expanded commerce.
  • The payoff was tangible: lower interest rates, increased available capital for productive enterprise, higher property values, and stronger conditions for agriculture, manufacturing, and the movement of goods.

Trucking, Logistics & Insurance Relevance These same foundations still matter for today’s supply chains. Predictable interest rates and stable credit conditions make fleet financing, trailer leases, and working capital more accessible and affordable for owner-operators and regional carriers. When public credit is sound, inflation surprises that spike diesel, parts, and labor costs become less frequent, supporting more reliable contract pricing and cash-flow planning. Hamilton recognized that public credit underpins private credit—the lifeblood of freight movement and just-in-time logistics.

When fiscal commitments are backed by credible repayment plans rather than perpetual rollover or inflationary erosion, expectations stabilize and credit flows more freely to productive sectors. Policy choices that favor short-term accommodations or concentrated interests without clear repayment mechanisms can instead generate volatility in costs and demand that hits thinner-margin transportation businesses hardest.

💰 Paying Debts Today: Credible Fiscal Backing for Price Stability and Credit Health

Modern analysis emphasizes that government debt remains sustainable only when backed by believable future surpluses or fiscal adjustments. Absent that commitment, inflation often becomes the adjustment mechanism that reduces the real burden of debt—disrupting price signals, eroding purchasing power, and complicating credit decisions throughout the economy.

  • Inflation and the value of money are tightly linked to whether fiscal policy provides a credible path to service and retire debt in real terms.
  • “Paying your debts” is therefore not merely a moral stance; it is a practical requirement for containing price volatility and preserving access to affordable credit.
  • Hamilton’s success demonstrated that establishing trust through responsible provision for obligations delivers lower long-term borrowing costs and broader economic vitality—benefits that extend directly to commercial transportation.

Trucking, Logistics & Insurance Relevance for SMEs in trucking and supply chains, fiscal-driven inflation shows up immediately in higher fuel, tire, maintenance, and wage costs that compress margins faster than many contracts can adjust. When shippers and receivers face their own margin pressure, payment delays and defaults rise—precisely the risk trade credit insurance is designed to mitigate. With protected receivables, carriers can continue offering competitive payment terms, maintain cash flow, and pursue growth even when macro conditions are uncertain. Credible fiscal discipline supports steadier freight volumes and more predictable financing environments for fleet modernization and technology adoption.

When repayment credibility is deprioritized in favor of short-term spending or targeted supports shaped by influential stakeholders, the resulting price and credit instability creates uneven headwinds—often burdening smaller, independent operators more than larger players with greater buffers or closer policy alignment.

Final Thought Hamilton proved that credible public credit is not a constraint on growth but its foundation. The same holds today: trucking and logistics SMEs perform best when inflation is contained, financing is predictable, and customer credit risk remains manageable. As your dedicated advisor in trade credit insurance and supply-chain risk management, I help transportation businesses translate these larger fiscal and credit dynamics into practical protection—safeguarding receivables, strengthening cash flow, and building resilience against policy-driven volatility.

Call-to-Action If you want to discuss tailored trade credit insurance solutions, a credit-risk review of key accounts in your freight network, or strategies to protect working capital amid shifting fiscal and inflationary conditions, I’m ready to help.

item.title: 🚛 Freight Under Pressure: Rising Trucking Costs, Global Collection Risks, and Hidden Credit Exposure
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The transportation and logistics sector continues to navigate a challenging environment marked by rising operating costs, persistent insolvency risk, and growing complexity in collecting receivables across borders. While freight markets show signs of stabilization, many businesses remain one customer failure away from a meaningful cash flow event.

For trucking companies, freight brokers, third-party logistics providers (3PLs), and their financial partners, understanding both operational risk and credit risk has never been more important.

🚚 Rising Transportation Costs Continue to Squeeze Margins

The American Transportation Research Institute's (ATRI) 2026 Operational Costs of Trucking report shows that carriers continue managing elevated operating expenses while profitability remains under pressure.

Key Insights

  • Average trucking operating costs reached record levels.
  • Repair and maintenance expenses continue rising.
  • Insurance costs remain elevated due to claims severity and litigation trends.
  • Many truckload operators are generating extremely thin operating margins.

Why This Matters

For trucking companies operating on margins below 1%, a single customer bankruptcy, payment default, or significant payment delay can wipe out annual profits.

As costs remain elevated, businesses have less capacity to absorb receivable losses. This makes customer credit quality and payment behavior increasingly important strategic considerations.

Risk Management Takeaway: Protecting Accounts Receivable is no longer just a credit function. It is becoming a core transportation profitability strategy.

Source: American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI), Operational Costs of Trucking 2026.

📦 3PL Growth Continues, But Customer Concentration Risk Is Rising

The logistics industry continues to consolidate as shippers place larger volumes with fewer strategic providers.

Key Insights

  • More shippers are increasing outsourced logistics spending.
  • Vendor consolidation continues across supply chains.
  • Large customers represent greater revenue concentration for many logistics providers.
  • Competition continues driving aggressive customer acquisition and credit extension.

Why This Matters

Revenue concentration can create hidden balance-sheet risk.

When a logistics company depends heavily on a small number of major accounts, the financial health of those customers becomes increasingly important.

If a large customer experiences financial distress, delayed payments can quickly affect:

  • Working capital
  • Payroll
  • Equipment investment
  • Fleet expansion plans

Risk Management Takeaway: Growth is valuable, but growth supported by quality receivables is far more sustainable.

🌎 International Debt Collection Is Becoming More Complex

A new Allianz Trade Collection Complexity Study covering 52 economies found that recovering commercial debt is becoming increasingly difficult amid global trade fragmentation, geopolitical uncertainty, insolvency growth, and regulatory complexity. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]

Key Insights

  • Germany, Netherlands, and Portugal rank among the easiest countries for debt recovery. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]
  • Saudi Arabia, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates rank among the most challenging. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]
  • Nearly 48% of international trade receivables are exposed to "Very High" or "Severe" collection complexity. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]
  • Insolvency proceedings represent the largest obstacle to successful debt recovery globally. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]

Why This Matters

As supply chains diversify and businesses expand internationally, the challenge is no longer simply getting paid.

The challenge is recovering money when something goes wrong.

Many companies discover collection obstacles only after:

  • A customer enters insolvency.
  • A dispute develops.
  • A foreign court becomes involved.
  • Legal costs erode recoveries.

Risk Management Takeaway: The cost of a bad debt often grows dramatically once international legal systems and insolvency proceedings become involved.

Source: Allianz Trade Collection Complexity Report 2026. [2026-01-27...tion-final | PDF]

💳 Credit Risk Has Been Relocated, Not Eliminated

Recent Allianz Research found that credit markets appear calm on the surface, but underlying risk has increasingly shifted rather than disappeared. [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]

Key Insights

  • Credit spreads remain historically tight despite deteriorating fundamentals. [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]
  • Risk has migrated into private credit and less transparent financing structures. [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]
  • Lower-rated borrowers continue facing pressure from higher borrowing costs. [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]
  • Financial stress often remains hidden until liquidity problems emerge. [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]

Why This Matters

Periods of easy credit often create a false sense of security.

When financial conditions tighten, businesses discover that risk was never eliminated. It was simply transferred elsewhere in the system, often into less visible corners of the economy.

At the same time, policy decisions, financing conditions, and capital allocation frequently favor larger institutions with privileged market access, leaving small and medium-sized enterprises exposed to sharper liquidity shocks.

For suppliers, transportation providers, and logistics companies, this reinforces a simple reality:

A sale is not complete until cash is collected.

Source: Allianz Research, Credit Risk Relocated, Not Removed (July 2026). [2026_07_02...entals_AZT | PDF]

✅ Final Thought

The transportation industry has always managed physical risk exceptionally well.

Today's challenge is managing financial risk.

As operating costs rise, margins tighten, and collection complexity increases, the ability to identify customer risk early and protect receivables can be the difference between growth and disruption.

Trade credit insurance is no longer just protection against bankruptcy. It is a strategic tool that helps companies:

  • Protect cash flow
  • Strengthen working capital
  • Expand safely
  • Navigate uncertain markets with confidence

The strongest transportation and logistics companies are not necessarily those with the most freight. They are often those with the most predictable cash flow.

item.title: Credit Risk Relocated, Not Removed
item.content:encoded:
Right now, the credit markets look calm. Spreads are tight, and growth numbers look okay. But the risk of companies failing to pay their bills has not gone away. It has just moved from one place to another.

Think of it like a Newton’s cradle — those hanging metal balls that transfer force from one end to the other. Risk is being passed along a chain: from safer companies (called Investment Grade or IG), through riskier public bonds (High Yield or HY), and into private loans (private credit). If you run a trucking, logistics, or transportation company, this matters a lot. Many of you have a big part of your money tied up in invoices that customers still owe you (accounts receivable). When your customers get into money trouble, you feel it fast. This easy-read guide explains what’s happening and what you can do about it.

Source: Allianz Research report from July 2, 2026. Written by Ludovic Subran and team. Extra numbers come from Bloomberg, S&P, Fitch, and others.

1. Things Look Fine on the Surface — But They’re Not as Strong as They Seem

Spreads (the extra money investors demand for taking risk) are very low right now — about 73 to 75 basis points. That is tighter than before the recent war fears. At the same time, companies are a bit weaker. Their ability to pay interest has dropped to about 6.3 times their earnings. Their debt levels have slowly risen.

Back in late 2019, companies had almost the same strength, but investors demanded a lot more extra money (about

110 basis points). Today, people are getting paid less for almost the same level of risk.

• Big buyers like insurance companies and pension funds keep buying because the overall interest rates look good to them.

• The Federal Reserve has not cut rates much. Old cheap loans are being replaced with more expensive ones. This keeps pressure on companies.

• Big tech companies are spending huge amounts on AI buildings and computers. That means more new debt coming to market soon.

Why trucking and logistics care: Your big customers may still look okay on paper. But if they take on more debt while rates stay high, their ability to pay you on time may weaken. Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) can protect the money they owe you.

2. The Biggest Danger: Companies Falling from Safe to Risky

The real problem sits in the lower part of the “safe” group (called BBB). These companies make up about 45% of the safer bond market. If they get downgraded to “risky,” big funds that can only own safe bonds have to sell them fast. That flood of selling hits the smaller, riskier market hard. Prices can drop much more than the actual change in quality warrants.

• In the 2020 stress time, these forced sales wiped out about 25 basis points of return — roughly one-third of today’s thin cushion.

• For three years straight, more companies have been downgraded than upgraded. The number of fallen companies is starting to rise again.

• With spreads already so tight, there is almost no room for error. Why trucking and logistics care: If a major shipper falls from safe to risky, payment terms can change overnight. Your unpaid invoices become riskier. Watching the lower end of the safe group and using Trade Credit Insurance gives you a real safety net.

3. High Yield Looks Better — But Only Because the Weakest Left

Normally when the economy slows, the riskier bond market (High Yield) is the first place people worry about. This time it actually looks a bit stronger than the bottom of the safe group. But that is mostly because the weakest companies have left.

The weakest borrowers moved into private loans and other private deals. What is left in public High Yield is cleaner— more BB-rated names and fewer of the very weakest (CCC). These bonds also have shorter lives, so their prices swing less.

• High Yield companies have kept their debt levels and interest coverage steadier than the BBB companies.

• The risk did not disappear. It just moved next door into private credit.

Why trucking and logistics care: Many private-equity-owned fleets, 3PLs, and logistics software companies now sit in the private market. When those private loans get into trouble, people often sell the easy-to-sell public High Yield bonds first. That can make freight-related credit spreads jump even if the public High Yield companies themselves are okay.

4. Private Credit: Where the Risk Went to Hide

Private credit is now a huge market — about $1.75 trillion. The weaker companies that left public High Yield did not vanish. They went into private loans. In private credit, values are estimated by people rather than priced daily by the market. That makes the trouble harder to see.

• These private borrowers carry a lot more debt (5 to 7 times earnings) and have thinner safety cushions (interest coverage of only 1 to 2 times).

• More companies are paying interest with more debt instead of cash (this is called Payment-In-Kind or PIK). That share has doubled to 8.9%. Lender takeovers of troubled companies jumped to $39 billion in the last two years — three times the previous three years combined.

• About one-quarter of these portfolios are in software and AI-related companies. Those deals were done when rates were near zero, and growth looked endless. Now AI is disrupting their own businesses.

• In private markets, there is no public rating drop. Trouble shows up as sudden stops on withdrawals, loan rewrites, or takeovers. The losses come later and in bigger chunks.

Why trucking and logistics care: Many logistics tech platforms, AI tools, and private-equity fleets use private credit. Rising PIK and takeovers mean some of them are already struggling to pay cash interest. When they run into trouble, your invoices may go unpaid. And when private investors need cash, they often sell public High Yield first — sending stress right back into markets you watch.

5. What This Means for You and Your Working Capital

The market is being held up more by strong buying demand than by truly strong company finances. That can change quickly. Here is the simple takeaway:

• The overall yield (interest rate plus spread) is still good enough to cover a moderate rise in risk premiums. Pure “extra return” is thin.

• The real weak spots are the lower-rated safe companies (BBB), the weakest High Yield names (CCC), and the older private loans made in 2021–2023 when everything looked easy.

• When fear hits, people sell what they can sell fastest — usually public High Yield. That means stress from private credit can spill over into public markets, even if those public companies are doing well.

Trucking & Logistics Takeaway: The risk of customers not paying remains. It has been moved and made harder to see. The smart move is simple: know which of your big customers sit in the riskier buckets, and protect the money they owe you with Trade Credit Insurance. Use Supply Chain Finance tools so your cash stays flexible when payment times stretch out.

6. Final Thought: Look Past the Calm Surface

Credit risk has not been removed. It has been passed along a chain from safer public bonds through high-yield bonds and into private loans. Different tricks hide the stress at each step. In a real scare, that hidden risk can come rushing back into the markets everyone can see.

For anyone who depends on customers paying their invoices — trucking, logistics, manufacturing, distribution — the lesson is clear: a calm surface and smooth private values do not mean everything is solid. The companies that win will treat risk as a full-circle job. They will combine regular insurance thinking with Trade Credit Insurance, which protects against unpaid invoices, and Supply Chain Finance, which keeps cash moving. Looking carefully at the weaker customers and older private deals, then adding real protection, turns this moving risk from a threat into something you can manage. As a Transportation Risk Specialist, I help trucking and logistics companies turn big-picture credit news into simple, practical steps that protect cash and support growth.

item.title: Fifth Year of Rising Insolvencies Looms: Middle East Spillovers Put Trucking & Logistics Supply Chains on High Alert for 2026
item.content:encoded:
The global economy is entering its fifth consecutive year of rising business insolvencies in 2026, with Allianz Research forecasting a +6% increase in the Global Insolvency Index — two percentage points higher than pre-conflict expectations. Spillovers from the Middle East crisis, including elevated oil and gas prices, disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and second-round inflation and confidence effects, are driving much of the upward revision and delaying any plateau until 2027.

For SME owners and operators in trucking, transportation, logistics, and supply chains, these are not distant macro trends. They translate directly into higher fuel and operating costs, unpredictable freight volumes from struggling retail and construction sectors, and elevated non-payment risk from buyers under margin pressure. Proactive risk management has never been more essential.

⛽ Energy Shocks & Supply Chain Pressure: The Immediate Hit to Freight Operations

•  Transportation ranks among the most vulnerable sectors to higher oil prices, supply-chain disruptions, and second-round effects (inflation, tighter financial conditions, and eroded confidence). Road transport, shipping, and related energy-intensive activities face immediate cost spikes that are difficult to fully pass through in competitive markets.

•  Broader value-chain impacts — from agrifood and manufacturing to healthcare and technology — create volatile demand patterns and potential delays that complicate capacity planning and lane profitability for carriers and 3PLs.

•  The combination of weaker demand in some lanes and structurally higher working capital needs leaves many SMEs exposed, especially those with thinner margins or higher debt loads.

Relevance to your operation: Fuel surcharges and contract flexibility become critical defenses. At the same time, rising buyer stress in downstream industries increases the chance of delayed or defaulted payments on your invoices.

📈 2026 Insolvency Outlook by the Numbers: What It Means for North American Freight

•  Global insolvencies are projected to rise +6% in 2026, with Asia (China +9%) remaining the largest contributor. North America shows contrasting trends: the US extends its rebound with +9% growth, while Canada continues declining (-4%).

•  Western Europe faces a prolonged rise (+3%, four points above pre-war forecasts), with most countries (10 of 17) showing only modest changes and thus sustaining elevated levels. Germany is seen rising +2% to roughly 24,650 cases; France +2% to about 69,900; the UK near-stable at -1% to around 26,550.

•  At the global level, the direct Middle East toll adds roughly +7,000 additional insolvency cases in 2026 (+700 in the US and +3,750 in Western Europe). Over 2.2 million jobs are at risk worldwide in 2026, concentrated in construction, retail, and services — key drivers of freight demand.

Relevance to your operation: Higher insolvency counts in customer-heavy sectors signal increased non-payment and domino risks through supplier networks. US-based trucking and logistics SMEs should expect sustained domestic pressure alongside global spillovers, making close monitoring of shipper and receiver credit health a priority.

⚠️ Downside Risks That Could Intensify the Pressure

•  A prolonged Middle East conflict could push global insolvencies close to +10% in 2026 and +3% in 2027, adding thousands more cases in the US and Western Europe through deeper energy and commodity shocks.

•  Additional amplifiers include a potential collapse in the current AI-driven boom (estimated +15,600 extra insolvencies across the US and Western Europe over 2026–2027) and fiscal confidence shocks tied to high sovereign debt levels (potentially +22,500 additional cases in Western Europe alone).

•  These scenarios would compound second-round effects — tighter credit, margin squeezes (especially in real estate and technology in Europe), and reduced pricing power — hitting firms with high working capital needs or limited buffers hardest.

Relevance to your operation: Scenario planning around extended energy volatility or sudden shifts in financial conditions helps identify which customer relationships carry outsized risk. These fiscal and policy dynamics often sustain cost pressures longer than expected, with independent operators in transportation absorbing more of the impact than larger entities with greater scale and access to mitigation tools.

🛡️ From Exposure to Protection: Practical Steps for SME Resilience

•  Large-firm insolvencies (already running at elevated quarterly levels) create ripple effects through extensive supplier networks, raising non-payment risk for smaller partners in the chain.

•  The post-pandemic surge in business formations has mechanically expanded the pool of firms that could become fragile under weaker conditions or external shocks, intensifying competition in many freight lanes.

•  With nearly two-thirds of monitored countries still above pre-pandemic insolvency levels entering 2026, the environment rewards ongoing vigilance over assumptions of quick normalization.

Relevance to your operation: Trade credit insurance stands out as a targeted solution that transfers buyer default risk, protects cash flow, and supports continued growth and credit extension even when macro conditions remain challenging. It is especially valuable for SMEs serving the retail, construction, and manufacturing sectors, or operating in cross-border supply chains, that are exposed to these interconnected pressures.

Final Thought

Sustained high levels of business insolvencies, amplified by geopolitical energy shocks and underlying fiscal headwinds, have become a defining feature of the current cycle rather than a temporary blip. For trucking, logistics, and supply-chain SMEs, the winners will be those who treat credit and operational risk management as strategic priorities — not afterthoughts. Understanding where the pressures are concentrated and deploying the right protections allows you to maintain stability and even capture opportunities as the landscape evolves.

Ready to stress-test your customer portfolio, review your current protections, or explore tailored trade credit insurance solutions that fit your trucking or logistics operation?

I’m here to help you navigate these risks with clarity and practical options.

item.title: Freight Under Pressure: Bankruptcies Rise, Costs Shift, and Policy Risks Build
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The freight market is sending mixed signals—demand is stabilizing, yet bankruptcies, layoffs, and policy shifts are accelerating. For carriers, brokers, and logistics firms, the real risk isn’t just volume—it’s cash flow, counterparty risk, and cost volatility .

Here’s what matters right now—and how smart operators are protecting downside while positioning for growth.

🚨 Freight Distress Is Rising—And Spreading Fast

  • A new wave of bankruptcies and layoffs is hitting transportation—from small carriers to large logistics firms [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Companies across trucking, warehousing, and brokerage are filing Chapter 7 (liquidation) and Chapter 11 (reorganization) amid high costs and financing pressure [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Hundreds of jobs have been cut, with shutdowns across freight, last-mile delivery, and air cargo services [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Earlier reports show more than 600+ jobs impacted in recent weeks alone , signaling sustained stress across the ecosystem [ freightwaves.com ]

Why it matters: Credit risk isn’t theoretical—it’s showing up in real-time failures. When margins compress and financing tightens, weak balance sheets break first. In this environment, growth without risk visibility becomes a liability.

📉 Layoffs Signal Structural Shifts in Logistics

  • Expeditors International is cutting 230 tech roles as part of a broader restructuring [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Revenue declines and rising operating costs are pushing even top-tier providers to reduce overhead [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Broader layoffs across DHL, GXO, FedEx, and others highlight system-wide cost discipline [ freightwaves.com ]

Why it matters: This isn’t just a cycle—it’s a reset. Companies are prioritizing profitability and liquidity over growth at all costs . That shift tends to expose weak customers faster—especially in B2B credit relationships.

⛽ Diesel Prices Drop—But Volatility Isn’t Gone

  • Diesel prices recently fell to roughly $5.05/gallon , down sharply after geopolitical tensions eased [ freightwaves.com ]
  • However, global supply is still expected to run in deficit, with inventories declining and production constrained [ freightwaves.com ]
  • Demand is weakening, but not enough to offset supply disruptions long term [ freightwaves.com ]

Why it matters: Lower fuel costs provide temporary margin relief—but volatility remains. Businesses relying on short-term price relief without hedging or planning could be caught off guard if prices rebound.

⚖️ New Labor Law Could Reshape Cost Structures

  • The Faster Labor Contracts Act passed the House, requiring union contracts within ~120 days—or government arbitration steps in [ freightwaves.com ]
  • This compresses negotiation timelines and could lead to contracts being set without full operational context [ freightwaves.com ]
  • The bill now moves to the Senate, where it faces a tighter political path [ freightwaves.com ]

Why it matters: For trucking companies, labor is one of the largest cost drivers. A faster path to unionization + binding arbitration = less pricing flexibility and more fixed cost risk .

🌍 The Bigger Economic Signal (What Most Are Missing)

  • Global policymakers are calling for “balanced growth” and reduced “imbalances”—often translating into more intervention in trade, capital flows, and pricing
  • Meanwhile, persistent government deficits and spending patterns are shaping inflation and capital allocation across markets
  • In plain terms: who finances growth—and how it’s repaid—matters more than short-term supply shocks

Why it matters for freight:

  • Credit cycles drive freight cycles
  • When capital tightens, bankruptcies rise
  • When liquidity expands without discipline, inflation and mispricing follow

This is why many firms are seeing demand recovery and financial distress at the same time —a classic late-cycle signal.

✅ Final Thought

The biggest risk in today’s freight market isn’t volume—it’s getting paid .

Between bankruptcies, cost volatility, and policy shifts, companies that win will be those that:

  • Know their customers’ financial strength
  • Protect receivables
  • Extend credit strategically—not blindly

That’s where trade credit insurance becomes less of a “nice-to-have” and more of a working capital strategy .

If you’re evaluating your exposure to customer defaults, tightening margins, or extending credit to grow safely—let’s connect.

I can share how companies in trucking, logistics, and manufacturing are:

  • Reducing bad debt risk
  • Improving cash flow predictability
  • Unlocking better financing terms

item.title: Supply Chain Cyber Attacks: A 2025–2026 Analysis with Focus on Trucking, Logistics, and SME Risk
item.content:encoded:
Supply chain cyber attacks exploit trusted relationships—software vendors, SaaS platforms, logistics service providers, identity systems, and open-source ecosystems—to gain initial access or broad downstream reach without directly targeting the ultimate victim. These attacks have evolved from opportunistic to strategic, leveraging speed, stealth (often malware-free), and AI to compress timelines from compromise to impact. In the transportation sector, where just-in-time operations, third-party platforms (TMS, ELDs, load boards, fuel cards, broker systems), and interconnected shipper-carrier-broker networks dominate, the consequences extend far beyond IT: they disrupt physical freight movement, trigger financial disputes, and strain working capital.

Key Trends and Statistics (2025 Data)

  • Explosive growth in logistics targeting : Cyberattacks tied to logistics rose 61% in 2025 (from 132 to 213 incidents) and have surged nearly 1,000% since 2021. Projections indicate they will double again in 2026 , with adversaries shifting from individual companies to shared transportation networks (ports, carriers, 3PLs, TMS providers).
  • Third-party involvement doubled : Verizon’s 2025 DBIR recorded third-party breaches rising from 15% to 30% of incidents—the largest single-year shift in the report’s history. Supply chain compromises now average $4.91 million in cost and take 267 days to identify and contain.
  • Software supply chain explosion : Over 454,600 new malicious open-source packages appeared in 2025 alone (+75% year-over-year). The npm ecosystem attacks proliferated, including the self-propagating ShaiHulud information stealer distributed via compromised packages.
  • Broad concern and blind spots : 88% of security leaders are concerned about supply chain cyber risks; nearly one-third of procurement managers reported increased attacks in the prior six months. Yet many organizations oversee only a small fraction of their extended (third-party) vendor ecosystem.
  • AI as accelerator : AI-driven threats now rank as the #1 supply chain risk for many leaders, used for personalized phishing, code generation, and evading safeguards.

These trends align with the CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report , which named supply chain attacks a defining tactic of the “Year of the Evasive Adversary.” Adversaries increasingly compromise upstream providers or code repositories to gain stealthy, scalable access rather than directly breaching well-defended endpoints. 82% of detections were malware-free , relying on valid credentials, trusted SaaS integrations, and inherited trust.

Prominent Tactics Observed

  1. Trojanized Software & Malicious Updates The most high-profile example: In February 2025, DPRK-nexus actor PRESSURE CHOLLIMA compromised Safe{Wallet} (a digital asset infrastructure provider). They pivoted from development credentials to the cloud environment, inserted malicious frontend elements, and stole $1.46 billion in cryptocurrency—the largest single reported financial theft via supply chain compromise (targeting Bybit exchange).
  2. Compromised Logistics & Freight Platforms Russian-linked phishing-as-a-service group Diesel Vortex (Sept 2025–Feb 2026) built dedicated infrastructure against freight systems, including DAT Truckstop, Penske Logistics, Timocom, and Electronic Funds Source (EFS) fuel cards. They used real-time credential harvesting (phishing + MFA bypass), posing risks of check fraud and double-brokering. Over 1,649 unique credentials were stolen from targeted logistics users.
  3. npm & Open-Source Dependency Attacks: Multiple campaigns in 2025 compromised JavaScript libraries and packages. One August incident used malicious Nx build packages to hijack victims’ local AI CLI tools (Claude, Gemini) to steal credentials and crypto. In November, 690 packages were compromised to spread the ShaiHulud stealer. These affect any organization (including logistics tech providers) relying on modern development pipelines.
  4. SaaS & Identity Supply Chain Compromise Attackers target centralized SaaS providers (TMS, broker platforms, cloud identity) to steal authentication tokens and pivot to subscriber networks. China-nexus actors and others exploit edge devices (VPNs, firewalls) as initial footholds into logistics-adjacent infrastructure.
  5. Social Engineering as Initial Access Vector. In trucking specifically, fake LinkedIn profiles (including “beautiful women” lures), vishing for password resets, and tailgating remain highly effective against distributed workforces (drivers, dispatch, brokers). These often serve as the entry point for deeper supply chain or ransomware operations.
  6. State-Nexus Espionage Russia’s Fancy Bear (APT28) targeted logistics and IT firms (air, maritime, rail, ports) supporting supply movements, using spear-phishing, credential harvesting, and custom malware. China-nexus groups showed an 85% increase in logistics targeting, often through rapid edge-device exploitation to enable persistent access and intelligence collection.

Impacts on Trucking & Logistics SMEs

  • Operational : TMS lockouts, disrupted routing/dispatching, ELD/fuel system issues, or broker platform fraud halt freight movement and trigger penalties or lost loads.
  • Financial Direct : Ransom demands, stolen funds/crypto, fraud (double-brokering, fake loads), regulatory fines from data breaches.
  • Cash Flow & Credit Ripple Effects : Downtime delays invoicing and collections. Disrupted partners may delay or dispute payments. Cargo fraud and impersonation schemes erode trust and create bad-debt exposure. Traditional cargo insurance frequently excludes cyber-related losses.
  • Reputational & Relationship : Loss of shipper/broker confidence; difficulty securing future loads or favorable terms.
  • SME Disproportionate Burden : Limited in-house security teams, heavy reliance on affordable third-party SaaS, and thinner margins mean that a single incident can threaten viability. Extended supply chains (third-party vendors) create visibility gaps.

Broader economic context amplifies these risks: rapid digitization of supply chains, interconnected platforms, and cost pressures have expanded attack surfaces while security investments often lag—particularly for smaller players.

Outlook for 2026

Supply chain attacks will remain a top threat. Expect continued AI enhancement of lures and tooling, more targeting of shared logistics networks, and experimentation with agentic/AI-autonomous elements. State actors will likely sustain logistics espionage tied to geopolitical supply monitoring. eCrime groups will refine platform-specific phishing and fraud schemes. Remediation lags (often 8+ days due to manual processes) and vendor blind spots will persist unless organizations adopt continuous third-party risk management.

Recommendations for Trucking & Logistics SMEs

  • Map and prioritize critical vendors (TMS, brokers, fuel, ELD, load boards) with due diligence and continuous monitoring.
  • Enforce least-privilege access, strong MFA (preferably phishing-resistant), and rapid patching of edge devices (ideally within 72 hours of critical disclosures).
  • Implement employee and driver training focused on social engineering and device integration risks.
  • Segment networks and monitor for anomalous SaaS/identity behavior.
  • Develop incident response plans that include financial continuity measures.
  • Consider specialized coverage: Cyber insurance for direct breach costs; Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) to protect against non-payment risks arising from partner disruptions or fraud; and Supply Chain Finance (SCF) to provide liquidity advances on receivables during recovery periods.

True resilience requires a 360-degree approach : technical defenses layered with financial safeguards. Cyber events in the supply chain frequently manifest as credit and cash-flow crises for SMEs. Trade Credit Insurance (TCI) and Supply Chain Finance (SCF) help bridge those gaps, allowing operations to continue while disputes or recoveries unfold.

If you would like a deeper dive into specific tactics, vendor risk frameworks, or how TCI/SCF can be structured for your book of business or client base, I am available to discuss tailored strategies.

Primary Sources

  • CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report (supply chain section, PRESSURE CHOLLIMA case, npm attacks, China-nexus logistics stats)
  • FreightWaves reporting on Diesel Vortex and trucking social engineering
  • Dark Reading / CISA on Fancy Bear logistics targeting
  • Verizon 2025 DBIR, IBM Cost of a Data Breach, Everstream Analytics, SecurityScorecard, Sonatype, and NMFTA transportation cybersecurity insights (via cited summaries)
